The analysis proceeds through five dimensions: the trust crisis organizations are creating through premature and performative AI deployment ("AI washing"); the choice architecture between automation by default and augmentation by design, drawing on the Acemoglu-Autor-Johnson framework and the three modes of human-AI collaboration (centaur, cyborg, self-automator); the broken talent pipeline that threatens the next generation of institutional expertise; the distributional consequences across gender, race, age, disability, geography, and income; and the governance frameworks available to each stakeholder.

The paper concludes with a prescriptive toolkit organized around two audiences: employers whose deployment decisions shape the workforce trajectory, and individuals navigating that trajectory as workers. The evidence supports a central conclusion: the barrier to effective AI adoption is not the workforce; it is the organizational environment. The window for building governance infrastructure that steers AI toward broadly shared benefit is open, and acting on the evidence available now is the distinguishing characteristic of organizations that lead transitions rather than being reshaped by them.

title: Infrastructure as Coordination and Capital-Formation: Toward a Unified Theory of the Infrastructure Feasibility Frontier and Revenue-Routed Settlement Logic

detail.title: Infrastructure as Coordination and Capital-Formation: Toward a Unified Theory of the Infrastructure Feasibility Frontier and Revenue-Routed Settlement Logic
detail.abstract: This document presents a unified research agenda arising from a systematic analysis of primary archival materials documenting Saudi Aramco's transportation and contractor development programs, 1942-1984. The empirical foundation-the William E. Mulligan Papers (Box 9, Folders 10 and 11) at Georgetown University's Booth Family Center for Special Collections, authenticated by Scott S. Taylor, Manuscripts Archivist; a 1983 Antenne 2 documentary archived at the Institut National de l'Audiovisuel, Paris; and four independently verified published sources-constitutes an unusually rich laboratory for institutional and financial economics. The agenda organizes around two unified theoretical concepts: the Infrastructure Feasibility Frontier, defined as the boundary of economic organizational forms made feasible by infrastructure systems embedding verification, threshold-setting, and market-creation; and Revenue-Routed Settlement Logic (RRSL), defined as a financial architecture combining embedded payment, automatic splitting, and condition-triggered disbursement, documented across six Aramco programs spanning 1942 to 1984 and predating modern fintech by forty to seventy-four years. Three research pillars emerge, generating eight specific papers. Beyond those eight papers, six additional financial mechanisms, seven independent economic phenomena, and four new research topics are identified and formally named for the first time. Th e founding paper of this agenda has been submitted for peer review.

title: Competition and Pass-Through of Market-Wide Cost Changes under Convex Costs
affiliations: Oxera Consulting LLP, Oxera Consulting LLP and

detail.title: Competition and Pass-Through of Market-Wide Cost Changes under Convex Costs
detail.abstract: Ritz (2024) argues that an increase in competition can reduce the rate of pass-through of market-wide cost changes when total cost is convex (C'' > 0, i.e., when there are diseconomies of scale). This article shows that, if competitive intensity rises, what is needed for passthrough to fall is a sufficiently strong marginal cost convexity C''' (i.e., a sufficiently hard capacity constraint), whereas if the number of firms rises, what is needed is that total cost concavity-C'' is sufficiently high (i.e., sufficiently strong economies of scale). Contrary to Ritz's argument, strong total cost convexity reinforces the standard result in either case.

title:
IHAV: Intraday Heterogeneous Autoregression with Anchored Volatility
Minute-Level Realized Volatility Forecasting for the S&P 500 Index
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title:
IHAV: Intraday Heterogeneous Autoregression with Anchored Volatility
Minute-Level Realized Volatility Forecasting for the S&P 500 Index

detail.abstract:
We develop IHAV (Intraday HAR with Adaptive Volatility), a real-time minute-by-minute realized volatility forecasting model for the S&P 500 index (SPX) over horizons of 5 to 60 minutes. The model combines Heterogeneous Autoregressive (HAR) features — lagged realized variance and cumulative intraday variance — with 0-day-to-expiration (0DTE) implied volatility calibrated against realized variance, and time-of-day session dummies. Estimated via Ridge regression in a strict expanding walk-forward framework on 426,000 SPX 1-minute bars (2019–2023), IHAV achieves R² = 0.815 at h = 30 minutes out-of-sample, outperforming a pure HAR benchmark (R² = 0.792), a naïve realized variance model (R² = 0.740), and standalone 0DTE implied volatility (R² = 0.510).

We document four main findings. First, the VIX index — the standard practitioner proxy for intraday volatility sizing — produces negative R² at all horizons (−0.85 to −1.37) and systematically overestimates intraday realized volatility by 10–11%, rendering it actively harmful as an intraday predictor. Second, calibrated 0DTE implied volatility and cumulative intraday realized variance are nearly identical (Pearson r = 0.995), confirming that short-dated options efficiently price current session volatility rather than providing independent forward information. Third, intraday session structure matters: the variance risk premium is maximum at lunch (84% positive, mean +0.040) and negative at the close, consistent with systematic option mispricing near expiry. Fourth, the residual signal delta-sigma = sigma_pred - sigma_lag exhibits monotone win-rate scaling with magnitude (65% to 90%), suggesting a tradable volatility direction edge with Kelly half-fractions of 4.6%–19.9% depending on signal strength.

The model survives the March 2020 COVID stress period (R² = 0.749 at VIX > 35) and shows no structural drift over 5 years. Extensions testing Bipower Variation and multi-DTE term structure features yield null results, confirming that calibrated ATM 0DTE implied volatility is the sufficient statistic for short-horizon SPX volatility.

title: Human-technology partnerships in the era of trucking automation: Findings from a multistakeholder workshop
affiliations: University of Massachusetts Amherst, University of Massachusetts Amherst, University of Massachusetts Amherst, University of Massachusetts Amherst, University of Massachusetts Amherst and University of Massachusetts Amherst

detail.title: Human-technology partnerships in the era of trucking automation: Findings from a multistakeholder workshop
detail.abstract: Automation and artificial intelligence (AI) are rapidly transforming commercial trucking, introducing advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) and autonomous driving systems (ADS) that reshape how driving work is organized, how safety is managed, and how human operators interact with increasingly capable technologies. Despite accelerating deployment, limited stakeholder-driven evidence exists that captures the experiences, expectations, and concerns of those most affected by this transition. This paper presents findings from a multistakeholder workshop convened during the 2025 AAA Foundation for Traffic Safety's Safe Mobility Conference, which brought together eleven participants representing academia, industry, and research organizations to examine human–technology partnerships in trucking automation. Using inductive thematic analysis of workshop transcripts and participant-generated materials, four interconnected themes were identified: (1) perceptions of AI, characterized by dynamic, context-dependent trust shaped by driver experience and occupational identity; (2) misalignment and risk in human–AI interaction, encompassing behavioral, institutional, and design-level gaps that generate compounding safety risks; (3) redefining the trucking workforce and driver role, reflecting anticipated occupational shifts toward system supervision and the uneven distribution of transition costs across carriers; and (4) building the conditions for human–AI teaming, synthesizing participant-generated recommendations for human-centered design, tiered training and certification pathways, and federal governance. Findings indicate that safe integration of AI in commercial trucking is a sociotechnical challenge requiring coordinated attention to interface design, workforce development, organizational capacity, and regulatory alignment.

title: When Host-Country Institutions Are Not Enough: Field-Level Governance and Formal Labor Standards Adoption among Suppliers in Latin America
affiliations: and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: When Host-Country Institutions Are Not Enough: Field-Level Governance and Formal Labor Standards Adoption among Suppliers in Latin America
detail.abstract: This article examines whether formal labor standards adoption among Latin American suppliers is more consistently associated with broad host-country institutional indicators or with field-level governance pressures. Using 832 supplier-level observations from 266 firms across eight countries during 2022–2025, the study compares Rule of Law and labor-rights conditions with coercive, normative, and mimetic field-level mechanisms. Fixed-effects, correlated random-effects/Mundlak, GEE AR(1), and robustness tests show that broad institutional indicators lack stable main-effect associations across estimators and sample compositions. Field-level governance mechanisms, especially coercive pressure, show more recurrent associations with formal labor standards adoption, while normative and mimetic mechanisms are more visible in between-firm comparisons and sensitivity analyses. The study contributes to institutional and global supply-chain research by locating supplier accountability within organizational fields. Findings are interpreted as conditional associations with formal ESG-based adoption, not causal effects or directly observed workplace implementation.

title: EDUCATIONAL AFFILIATATIONS OF FEMALE CORPORATE DIRECTORS IN FAMILY CONTROLLED FIRMS: A GEOGRAPHICAL ANALYSIS
affiliations: Nipissing University

detail.title: EDUCATIONAL AFFILIATATIONS OF FEMALE CORPORATE DIRECTORS IN FAMILY CONTROLLED FIRMS: A GEOGRAPHICAL ANALYSIS
detail.abstract: Research examining the locations of boards of directors contributes to our understanding of corporations. This study adds to this field through an investigation female directors of family-controlled firms (FCFs). It investigates the geography between the boards of directors of companies and the universities attended by these individuals. The spatial relationship investigates the locations of universities and corporate headquarters. It was found that females that sat on FCFs are more likely to have more distant educations than females that sat on NonFCFs. On the other hand, female directors of FCFs attained post-secondary educations closer than male directors of FCFs. The spatial affiliation is particularly relevant to concept of institutionalism in economic geography. When individuals are exposed to different institutional structures, valuable knowledge is gained, perhaps more valuable than knowledge gained at local universities. This line of reasoning contends that local universities maintain and teach similar approaches, which personnel from local firms already know. On the other hand, outside institutions can offer novel corporate strategies.

title: Governing Intangible Assets across Institutional Spaces The Standardization-Adaptation Frontier and Channel Choice in International Retail
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Governing Intangible Assets across Institutional Spaces The Standardization-Adaptation Frontier and Channel Choice in International Retail
detail.abstract: This paper models the global standardization-adaptation trade-off as a firm-level optimization problem within the frameworks of Industrial Organization and Transaction Cost Economics. Using an empirical qualitative case study methodology focused on international fashion retailer Parfois, we analyze how a multinational enterprise minimizes unit production costs via economies of scale while mitigating local market frictions and information asymmetries. We investigate how specific intangible assets -corporate name, product portfolio, positioning, and brand origin - are managed across diverse regulatory and culturais regimes. Findings reveal that this corporate strategy is non-binary. Centralized governance maximizes minimum efficient scale through global standardization, while selective market differentiation via local adaptation serves as a tactical market-capture mechanism. This strategic posture is determined dynamically by cost structures, technological maturity, and market complexity. Ultimately, we propose a framework of modern operational balance, demonstrating how Industry 4.0 technologies bridge high-efficiency scale and customized cross-border performance under conditions of varying operational and demand-side heterogeneity.

title: Risk-Based Collaborative Planning for Cyber-Physical-Social Distribution Systems Against Extreme Weather
affiliations: Wuhan University of Technology, Wuhan University of Technology, Wuhan University of Technology, Wuhan University of Technology, Wuhan University of Technology and Huazhong University of Science and Technology

detail.title: Risk-Based Collaborative Planning for Cyber-Physical-Social Distribution Systems Against Extreme Weather
detail.abstract: The integration of peer-to-peer (P2P) energy trading offers a promising pathway to enhance distribution system resilience against extreme weather. However, the efficacy of this social layer is strictly contingent upon the survivability of the cyber layer. To address the vulnerability where communication outages precipitate market fragmentation and exacerbate load shedding, a resilience-oriented collaborative stochastic planning framework for cyber-physical-social systems (CPSS) is proposed. First, the cross-domain cascading failure mechanism is modeled, quantifying how cyber interruptions block social transactions and subsequently impact physical power balance. On this basis, a bi-level collaborative planning model is established to co-optimize pre-disaster resource configuration: the upper level determines the optimal hardening strategies for communication infrastructure and physical lines to minimize tail risks, while the lower level optimizes the capacity configuration of distributed generation and energy storage systems. A nested progressive hedging and alternating direction method of multipliers (PH-ADMM) algorithm is utilized to solve the multi-scenario stochastic problem efficiently. Numerical case studies on modified IEEE 33-node and 123-node systems validate that the proposed collaborative planning strategy significantly enhances system resilience by ensuring the cyber-connectivity of critical market agents.

title: A Systematic Bibliometric Review of Arbitrage and Market Efficiency in Indian Options Trading
affiliations: Punjab Agricultural University

detail.title: A Systematic Bibliometric Review of Arbitrage and Market Efficiency in Indian Options Trading
detail.abstract: This study represents a comprehensive view of bibliometric analysis of global research on the arbitrage efficiency in the options market from 2001-2025. The data set include 1548 articles from open access journals, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar. This study identifies most influential authors, publication trends, most prominent journals, countries, institutions a thematic area. Most of the early work was based on theoretical concepts, pricing models and tested in developed markets but now empirical studies have gained more popularity especially in countries like India. This review provides a roadmap for future research as it identifies gaps in the literature, particularly within India. The findings also provide insights to academics, policymakers and market participants who aim to understand and improve arbitrage efficiency in financial markets.

title: Congestion Pricing in Low-Altitude Airspace: A Stackelberg Approach to UTM Markets
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Congestion Pricing in Low-Altitude Airspace: A Stackelberg Approach to UTM Markets
detail.abstract: ​The rapid expansion of drone operations is turning low-altitude airspace into an economically significant but increasingly congested resource. Although the Unmanned Traffic Management (UTM) literature has advanced substantially in operational, safety, and interoperability issues, the economic mechanisms required to price airspace, regulate market entry, and internalize congestion externalities remain largely underdeveloped. This paper addresses that gap by proposing an analytical framework in which the regulator and competing drone operators interact as a two-stage Stackelberg game. In the base formulation, the regulator sets a unit tariff to maximize regulatory revenue; in the extended formulation, the regulator adopts a Pigouvian stance, internalizing congestion externalities that scale with aggregate traffic density. We derive closed-form expressions for the equilibrium tariff, market quantity, and operator profits, and we prove that the optimal congestion-aware tariff is strictly increasing in the regional congestion parameter, providing a theoretical foundation for spatially and temporally differentiated pricing. The model is calibrated with 2025 operational data from SARPAS the Brazilian national UTM platform administered by DECEA and its robustness is assessed through Monte Carlo simulation over stochastic demand and cost parameters. The results reveal a fundamental trade-off: increased competition enhances allocative efficiency and price stability but erodes the regulator’s revenue base and amplifies the sensitivity of welfare to congestion costs. The empirical calibration shows that congestion-efficient tariffs in dense urban cells (São Paulo) are 40–60% higher than a uniform national tariff, a magnitude that uniform pricing cannot accommodate without substantial efficiency losses. These findings contribute to the transport-economics, market-design, and UTM literatures by integrating strategic regulation, congestion externalities, and empirical calibration within a single framework, and they offer actionable guidance for the design of scalable, financially sustainable UTM systems.

title: Post-Disaster Road Network Resilience under Mixed Traffic with Connected and Autonomous Vehicles
affiliations: University of Auckland, University of Auckland - Faculty of Engineering and The University of Auckland

detail.title: Post-Disaster Road Network Resilience under Mixed Traffic with Connected and Autonomous Vehicles
detail.abstract: Connected and autonomous vehicles (CAVs) are expected to reshape future traffic operations, but their contribution to road network resilience during large-scale disruptions remains underexplored. This study develops a microscopic traffic simulation framework to evaluate regional road network resilience under varying CAV penetration levels and post-disaster recovery stages. A hypothetical Wellington Fault earthquake scenario is adopted to represent network disruption. Resilience is assessed using connectivity and serviceability indicators, together with travel time and generalized system cost accounting for completed and unserved demand. Results show that CAV benefits depend strongly on network state and recovery stage. While CAVs have limited influence under fully operational or highly fragmented, low-density conditions, higher penetration levels improve throughput and reduce delays in partially restored, oversaturated networks. The findings demonstrate that conventional travel-time measures can underestimate system-wide impacts when substantial demand cannot be immediately served. The results provide insights for post-disaster recovery planning and future mixed-traffic operations.

title: Autonomy in the Periphery: Post-Acquisition Governance of Japanese MNC Subsidiaries in Europe
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Stockholm School of Economics

detail.title: Autonomy in the Periphery: Post-Acquisition Governance of Japanese MNC Subsidiaries in Europe
detail.abstract: Japanese multinational corporations (MNCs) have traditionally relied on greenfield investments and tightly controlled subsidiaries, but cross-border acquisitions have become an increasingly important entry mode. Prior research has focused on post-acquisition integration in major host economies, with limited attention to governance in peripheral contexts. This study examines post-acquisition governance and subsidiary autonomy in Japanese MNC acquisitions in Sweden, conceptualized as a peripheral European location. Drawing on headquarters–subsidiary relations and subsidiary role perspectives, we analyze how parent firms structure control and coordination. The findings show that Japanese MNCs grant high levels of autonomy, characterized by limited headquarters intervention, substantial discretion over resources, and reduced reliance on expatriate control. Instead, governance is based on trust and respect for subsidiary capabilities. We argue that this reflects a shift toward autonomy-based governance, where control is relaxed to preserve and leverage subsidiary-specific advantages in peripheral contexts, extending understanding of control–autonomy dynamics in MNCs.

title: Association between Hospital Bed Attainment Rates and the Density of Healthcare Professionals in Japan: A Nationwide Ecological Study
affiliations: Tohoku University, Saga University and Tohoku University

detail.title: Association between Hospital Bed Attainment Rates and the Density of Healthcare Professionals in Japan: A Nationwide Ecological Study
detail.abstract:
Background: 
In Japan, the ”Regional Healthcare Plan” aims to optimize the allocation of hospital beds based on projected healthcare demand. However, many regions fail to achieve the recommended bed attainment rates, suggesting that factors beyond demand, particularly healthcare workforce supply, may influence regional disparities. 

Methods: 
We conducted a nationwide cross-sectional ecological study using publicly available data. The unit of analysis was the secondary medical field. Hospital bed attainment rates were calculated as the ratio of actual to required beds and were categorized into three groups for each bed function. Group comparisons were performed using the Kruskal–Wallis test with Bonferroni correction, and associations were assessed using Spearman’s rank correlation coefficients. 

Results: 
Bed attainment rates varied widely across regions, particularly for intensive and acute care beds. High total bed attainment rates were associated with a high density of nonphysician professionals, including nurses and rehabilitation staff. Intensive care bed attainment rates were positively associated with physicians and pharmacists. By contrast, acute care bed attainment rates were negatively correlated with physician and pharmacist densities. Inpatient rehabilitation and chronic care bed attainment rates were positively associated with the density of multiple nonphysician professionals, such as therapists, dietitians, and care workers. 

Conclusion: 
The relation between hospital bed attainment rates and healthcare workforce density varies substantially according to bed function. These findings suggest that effective regional healthcare planning should incorporate not only projected demand but also the composition and distribution of the healthcare workforce to avoid mismatches between bed capacity and service delivery.

title: Diagnosing and Governing Nascent Space Sectors: A National Space System Framework from Peru

detail.title: Diagnosing and Governing Nascent Space Sectors: A National Space System Framework from Peru

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author reports there are no competing interests to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study. The research is based exclusively on the analysis of publicly available documents, including government legislation, official institutional reports, academic publications, and policy documents. The study did not involve human participants, animal subjects, personal data, or clinical trials, and therefore did not require institutional ethics committee approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The underlying master's thesis at the Universidad de San Martín de Porres (Lima, Peru) was self-funded by the author. No external funding supported the preparation of this article.

detail.abstract: The governance structures required to coordinate space activities in developing countries remain understudied, despite evidence that the binding constraint on space development in these nations is institutional rather than technical. This article examines Peru's space sector through a qualitative research design, applying an assessment instrument adapted from the Space Mission and Management Ladder 1 and enriched with governance indicators absent from the original tool. The evaluation places Peru at a medium development level: the country operates an earth observation satellite and maintains cooperation agreements with NASA, yet lacks both a national space policy and an institutional architecture to coordinate its expanding activities. Ten governance challenges, grouped into two categories, show that technical capabilities remain fragmented and underutilized when no governance structures connect them. The article proposes a National Space System (SNE), a multi-actor governance model integrating institutional architecture, policy instruments, and participatory mechanisms. The proposal is validated against the governance approaches of Mexico, Colombia, and Chile, drawing lessons on policy completeness, stakeholder inclusion, civil-military transitions, and political continuity. Developments including the 2026 congressional approval of a spaceport initiative, 2 the signing of the Artemis Accords, 3 and the entry into force of the ALCE convention 4 confirm the timeliness of these findings.

title: Chaotic Three-Body Retaliation in the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma: A Strategy Grounded in Deterministic Chaos and Dual-Process Cognition

detail.title: Chaotic Three-Body Retaliation in the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma: A Strategy Grounded in Deterministic Chaos and Dual-Process Cognition

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study involves only computational simulation and does not include human participants, patient data, or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes and analyzes a novel strategy for the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma (IPD) termed Chaotic Three-Body Retaliation (RC3C). The strategy combines unconditional initial cooperation with a probabilistic retaliation mechanism whose intensity grows exponentially with the number of defections suffered, and whose perround realization is determined by a chaotic dynamical system inspired by the gravitational Three-Body Problem. Unlike conventional stochastic strategies, RC3C does not operate with fixed, stationary probabilities: it integrates a structured memory of interaction history, a sensitization parameter governing the speed of transition from cooperation to retaliation, and a chaotic number generator whose initial conditions depend on external variables inaccessible to the opponent. We argue that this architecture models the dynamic transition between the two cognitive systems described by Kahneman-the deliberative and the automatic-mediated by the neurobehavioral sensitization documented by Sapolsky, implemented through the structural unpredictability identified by Lorenz and Poincaré in deterministic non-linear systems. Results from a round-robin tournament simulation against nine classical reference strategies (50 repetitions, 200 rounds per match, seed 42) demonstrate performance competitive with Tit-for-Tat and Grudger, outperforming Pavlov, Generous TFT, and all non-cooperative strategies.

title: From Cost-Effectiveness to Contextual Fit: Adapting Blockchain Traceability Frameworks from UK Food Supply Chains to the Nigerian Market

detail.title: From Cost-Effectiveness to Contextual Fit: Adapting Blockchain Traceability Frameworks from UK Food Supply Chains to the Nigerian Market

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial conflict of interest in relation to this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is a conceptual and framework study based entirely on secondary data and published literature. No human participants, patient data, or primary data collection was involved. Ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently as an extension of postgraduate research completed at the University of Hull, United Kingdom.

detail.abstract:
Purpose: Recent research has demonstrated that blockchain-based traceability systems outperform traditional track-and-trace infrastructure on cost-effectiveness grounds within developed market contexts, particularly in UK food supply chains. However, the structural conditions underpinning this cost advantage reliable digital connectivity, formal supply chain actors, and established regulatory frameworks differ fundamentally in emerging markets. This paper examines how the cost-effectiveness case for blockchain traceability must be reconceptualised for the Nigerian food supply chain context, and proposes a contextualised implementation framework adapted to Nigerian structural realities.

Design/methodology/approach: The paper adopts a conceptual framework development approach, grounded in evidence synthesis from: (1) the authors' prior systematic review of blockchain in UK food supply chains (Odukwu, 2025); (2) secondary data on the Nigerian logistics and food supply chain sector; and (3) relevant literature on blockchain deployment in low-resource and emerging market contexts. The Nigerian Contextual Fit Framework (NCFF) is proposed as a structured tool for evaluating and adapting blockchain traceability architectures for Nigerian deployment. 

Findings: The paper finds that while the cost-effectiveness arguments for blockchain traceability hold in principle for Nigerian food supply chains, where post-harvest losses of approximately 40% and food fraud impose enormous economic and social costs. The architectural assumptions underpinning UK blockchain deployments are largely inapplicable. Nigerian FSCs are characterised by informality, low connectivity, energy instability, weak regulatory enforcement, and dominance of smallholder farmers and market traders. A mobile-first, lightweight distributed ledger architecture, community-based verification mechanisms, and USSD-compatible interfaces are proposed as contextually appropriate alternatives to the sensor-intensive, internet-dependent models deployed in UK and US retail supply chains. 

Originality/value: This paper makes the first systematic attempt to apply UK blockchain traceability evidence to the Nigerian FSC context, filling a gap in literature that is dominated by large-market or Asian studies. The Nigerian Contextual Fit Framework (NCFF) provides a practical and theoretically grounded tool for policymakers, technology developers, and NGOs seeking to deploy blockchain traceability in West African food systems.

title:
Existential Management

Ontological Architecture of the Organization and the Meaning of the Organization as the Core of Integrative Stability
affiliations: Independent Researche

detail.title:
Existential Management

Ontological Architecture of the Organization and the Meaning of the Organization as the Core of Integrative Stability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this theoretical paper.
declarations.funderStatement: The author received no external funding for this research.

keywords: Ontological Limit of the Organization’s Existence

detail.abstract:
Existential Management is a socio-ontological framework that interprets organizations as structures of coordinated decision-making whose identity and stability depend on the continuous reproduction of the meaning of the organization over time.

This White Paper presents the ontological architecture of the organization as a unity of decision-making and formulates the fundamental thesis according to which the meaning of the organization is a constitutive condition of the identity of the organization.

The document develops the concept of the meaning of the organization as the ontological core of identity, distinguishes its content and form, analyzes the distribution of meaning in the social consciousness of the organization, and describes the cascade of meaning as a structural flow through which the meaning of the organization becomes ontologically effective in decision-making and action.

The framework also includes an ontological justification of entropic drift as an inherent tendency of collective decision-making toward fragmentation and the concept of integrative force as the dynamic capacity of the organization to maintain unity of decision-making over time.

The text also clarifies the epistemological status of the framework as an ontological architecture, not an empirical explanatory theory, and differentiates Existential Management from systems theory, sensemaking theory, and institutional theory of organization.

The framework is articulated through an axiomatic structure and supplemented by a diagnostic architecture of stability, which enables structural analysis of the coherence of decision-making, the distribution of meaning, the continuity of the cascade of meaning, and the trend of integrative force over time.

title: Does Divisia Money Growth Influence Business Inventory Levels
affiliations: University of Northern Iowa and University of Northern Iowa

detail.title: Does Divisia Money Growth Influence Business Inventory Levels
detail.abstract: Do changes in the money supply influence how much inventory firms hold? Understanding what drives inventory accumulation matters for both firms managing supply chains and policymakers monitoring business cycle dynamics, as inventory swings are a well-documented amplifier of economic expansions and recessions. This paper examines whether Divisia M4 money growth helps predict business inventory growth using monthly U.S. data from January 1993 to December 2024 (1993M01-2024M12), with 384 observations (383 after differencing). A multiple regression model and a time series ARIMA model are employed for predictive performance evaluation. The regression results point to an economically large coefficient of-1.664 (OLS significant; HAC p = 0.193) for Divisia M4 growth, implying that a higher broad money growth is associated with less inventory accumulation, consistent with a demand-pull effect that reduces existing stocks. The regression model accounts for 25.8% of the variation in inventory growth with an in-sample RMSE of 0.4756 and out-of-sample cross-validated RMSE of 0.5052. The ARMA(1,1) model outperforms the regression model with an expanding-window RMSE of 0.4495, suggesting superior pure forecasting accuracy. These results suggest that while Divisia money growth is a statistically significant determinant of inventory behavior, short-run inventory dynamics are also influenced by interest rates, inflation and consumer sentiment, emphasizing the usefulness of monitoring broad monetary aggregates in addition to conventional indicators for supply chain and business cycle forecasting.

title: Permitting Delays, Regulatory Regimes, and Investment: Evidence from the Clean Water Act

detail.title: Permitting Delays, Regulatory Regimes, and Investment: Evidence from the Clean Water Act
detail.abstract: This paper develops a framework for measuring how changes in federal environmental permitting requirements affect private investment. We use longitudinal variation in Clean Water Act (CWA) jurisdictions-generated by a sequence of Supreme Court decisions and administrative rules between 2015 and 2026-to estimate the effect of regulatory stringency on the time-to-build distribution of planned electric generation projects. Project phases are observed in the Energy Information Administration's monthly 860M database, allowing us to estimate a Discrete Phase-Type (DPH) hazard model in which the CWA regulatory regime shifts each project's exit hazard and approval rate. We find that stricter CWA regulation slows the permitting phase and reduces the probability of a successful exit, while the Sackett v. EPA (2023) decision, which narrowed CWA jurisdiction, reverses these effects. We embed the estimated timeto-build distributions in a structural model of capital investment in which permitting delays raise the user cost of capital and discourage entry. Simulating the Sackett decision for solar energy projects, we estimate a long-run elasticity of investment with respect to a reduction in permitting duration of approximately-0.36.

title: A Theory of Inefficiency Distributions
affiliations: Maastricht University and Maastricht University - School of Business and Economics

detail.title: A Theory of Inefficiency Distributions
detail.abstract: We develop a simple theory of the distribution of technical inefficiency. In our model, the joint forces of innovation, imitation and the refined use of existing technologies determine the shape and spread of inefficiency in the cross section. The theory yields clear patterns. When innovation arrives discontinuously, the inefficiency distribution transitions through a zero-inflated truncated normal shape and ultimately collapses to a point mass. Imitation and convergence mainly change the overall dispersion but rarely the qualitative shape class. However, when innovation is continuous, then the inefficiency distribution converges to a (left-truncated) normal form. These results matter for empirical work: in stochastic frontier analysis the assumed inefficiency distribution is not an innocuous convenience but an identifying choice that influences estimated technology, returns to scale, and technical change. We provide diagnostics and a theory-based menu of distributions that help researchers avoid misspecification.

title: Self-Deception and the Structure of Moral Awareness: A Theological Account of Culpability and the Noetic Effects of Sin

detail.title: Self-Deception and the Structure of Moral Awareness: A Theological Account of Culpability and the Noetic Effects of Sin
detail.abstract: This article argues that self-deception is not a logical paradox of simultaneously knowing and not knowing, but a structured impairment of moral awareness. Drawing on the doctrine of the noetic effects of sin (Romans 1:18) and an exegesis of 2 Peter 3:5-where persons are said to 'deliberately overlook' what they know-it proposes a three-tier account: pre-reflective limitation, volitional non-attending, and active suppression. These tiers form a continuum of increasing volitional involvement, allowing for a more precise correlation between moral responsibility and an agent's capacity for awareness. The conclusion suggests that the noetic effects of sin deform the structure of awareness itself, such that the recovery of moral knowledge requires the reordering of attention and the will.

detail.abstract: Cryptoassets, while viewed by many as a significant innovation in the banking and investment industry, present exigent risks to investors, markets and possibly the financial system itself. Can these risks be managed appropriately using securities regulation? This article argues that securities regulation is appropriate to regulate a popular kind of cryptoasset, utility tokens, given the similarities between utility token risks and those found in traditional securities markets. This analysis begins to point to a consistent global regulatory response to cryptoasset regulation and has implications for future cryptoassets and financial innovation more generally.

title: Data-Driven Decision Making and Sales Growth in FMCG Companies in Bangladesh: A Conceptual Review and Research Agenda
affiliations: East West University and North South University

detail.title: Data-Driven Decision Making and Sales Growth in FMCG Companies in Bangladesh: A Conceptual Review and Research Agenda
detail.abstract: This paper examines how data-driven decision making can support sales growth in fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) companies in Bangladesh. The manuscript is positioned as a conceptual review article rather than an empirical study. It synthesizes research on analytics capability, retail analytics, demand forecasting, promotion optimization, distribution execution, and organizational readiness, then interprets these insights in the context of Bangladesh's FMCG market. The review suggests that data-driven decision making affects sales growth through four linked mechanisms: stronger customer insight, better demand forecasting, more effective promotion decisions, and tighter distribution execution. The paper also argues that the sales effect of data is conditional rather than automatic. Data quality, managerial commitment, employee capability, and an analytical culture shape whether data is translated into timely commercial action. The article contributes in three ways. First, it consolidates fragmented literature into one Bangladesh-relevant framework. Second, it explains why the FMCG context requires fast, outlet-level, evidence-based decisions. Third, it proposes a research agenda for future empirical work in Bangladesh. The paper concludes that FMCG firms can improve sales growth when they move beyond routine reporting and use data as a decision infrastructure across forecasting, promotion, and route-to-market management.

title: Empirically Grounded Finite Horizon Multipliers for Privately Held Business Appraisal

detail.title: Empirically Grounded Finite Horizon Multipliers for Privately Held Business Appraisal

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The computational work in this article was developed in collaboration with Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant. All methodology, data source selection, and analytical judgments are the author's.

detail.abstract: This article shows that the Gordon Growth Model systematically overstates terminal values of mature businesses. It proposes an empirically grounded replacement for the Gordon Growth terminal value in privately held business appraisal. The replacement is operationally identical to the Gordon Growth formula (GGF)-a single multiplier applied to normalized cash flow-but derived from observed sector survival data rather than a perpetuity assumption. The multiplier table underlying this framework was developed in collaboration with Claude (Anthropic) derived from U.S. Census Bureau Business Dynamics Statistics for mature firms across seven sectors, four revenue size bands, sixteen attained ages, and nine hurdle rates. The computational scale of this table development was not practically achievable by a single researcher working manually before AI-assisted computation made it feasible.

title: Digital Capital, Artificial Intelligence, and Education in Sub-Saharan Africa
affiliations: Université Paris Est Créteil (UPEC)

detail.title: Digital Capital, Artificial Intelligence, and Education in Sub-Saharan Africa
detail.abstract: The rapid advance of artificial intelligence (AI) in education outpaces the data needed to assess its impact. Large-scale international surveys do not yet measure schools' actual exposure to AI, making direct causal estimation impossible. This article proposes an alternative strategy-prospective and distributive-to evaluate ex ante the risks of deploying AI in highly stratified school systems. Using PASEC 2019 micro-data from fourteen sub-Saharan African countries, we construct two school-level indices: a digital capital index and a socio-educational vulnerability index. A within-country quadrant typology and a triple-risk indicator reveal that disadvantaged students are overwhelmingly concentrated in schools with low digital capital and high vulnerability-environments where converting AI into learning gains is least plausible. Estimates findings show that digital capital is positively associated with mathematics achievement, vulnerability exerts a penalizing effect, and returns to digital capital vary substantially across schools and territories, with partly compensatory effects emerging in peri-urban areas. Interpreted through the lens of Rawls's difference principle, these findings indicate that educational AI functions as a conditional amplifier: without explicit targeting and complementary investments in conversion capacity, its deployment risks widening existing inequalities.

title: The Patronage Equilibrium: Political Selection, Institutional Path-Dependence, and India's Growth Constraints

detail.title: The Patronage Equilibrium: Political Selection, Institutional Path-Dependence, and India's Growth Constraints
detail.abstract: India's economic expansion has been impressive in scale but shallow in depth-factor accumulation has outpaced the productivity, employment, and innovation gains observed in the East Asian late-industrialisers. This paper traces the gap to a self reinforcing political-selection equilibrium with four interlocking traps. Contesting elections requires large private outlays, which produce adverse selection in the candidate pool toward citizens with liquid wealth or coercive capacity. Ministerial portfolios are recurrently used to recoup these outlays through discretionary allocation and regulatory selectivity, while apex bureaucratic, judicial, and media institutions exercise autonomy more freely on low-stakes than high-stakes cases. Association for Democratic Reforms data show that 46% of 18th Lok Sabha members have declared criminal cases, and such candidates win at roughly three times the rate of clean candidates. The argument is anchored against two comparator groups-the four North-East Asian technology-intensive economies as a frontier-technology benchmark, and three large emerging-market democracies (Indonesia, Brazil, Mexico) as political peers. The reading complements rather than substitutes for factor-based and macro-policy accounts, and points to a multi-margin reform agenda that pairs electoral-finance, candidate screening, and allocation-procedure reforms with digital-governance instruments whose effects on each trap can be assessed empirically.

detail.abstract: This study develops an integrated Business Intelligence (BI) and econometric framework for forecasting industrial chemical imports, validated through the case of Vietnam's Sodium Hydroxide (NaOH) market (HS Code 28151200). Utilizing a high-frequency dataset of 1,993 customs transactions spanning December 2024 to April 2025-capturing 113,466 metric tons of NaOH valued at USD 41.4 million across 146 importers and 108 exporters-the research synthesizes transaction-level trade records with macroeconomic drivers including Vietnam's Industrial Production Index (IPI), GDP growth, VND/USD exchange rate and global caustic soda price benchmarks. A hybrid forecasting architecture combining log-linear structural demand estimation, Seasonal ARIMA and Vector Autoregression (VAR) is developed and validated. The proposed framework achieves a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 6.2%, substantially outperforming traditional ARIMA (12.4%) and OLS (10.8%) benchmarks. VAR impulse response analysis confirms a statistically significant negative response of import volumes to exchange rate shocks, with a trough at Month 3 and an IPI spillover effect persisting for six months. The study makes three original contributions: (1) the first application of transaction-level customs data to econometric NaOH import demand modeling in Vietnam; (2) a validated hybrid ARIMA-VAR forecasting architecture; and (3) a replicable BI operationalization framework translating econometric outputs into procurement decision support. Results demonstrate that IPI and downstream industrial output are the dominant demand drivers, with a short-run price elasticity of-0.41 and exchange rate elasticity of-0.32. The framework is scalable to other HS-coded industrial inputs across emerging markets.

title: The Heterogeneity Imperative: AI, Machine Learning, Conjoint Analysis, and the Unfinished Agenda of Wagner Kamakura
affiliations: Independant and Rice University

detail.title: The Heterogeneity Imperative: AI, Machine Learning, Conjoint Analysis, and the Unfinished Agenda of Wagner Kamakura

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Author Yang Wang is an employee of Amazon; however, this chapter is unaffiliated with any work at Amazon.

detail.abstract: This chapter evaluates the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) on conjoint analysis through the lens of Wagner Kamakura’s "heterogeneity imperative." While AI/ML methods often match population averages, they frequently fail to uncover the underlying structure of consumer heterogeneity—defined here as taste, structural, and concomitant variable differences. The authors assess four key applications: machine-learning-driven adaptive design and generative product design (which respect heterogeneity), large language model (LLM) synthetic respondents (which destroy it via "flattening" and stereotyping), and deep-learning flexible utility estimation (which partially recovers it). To address these methodological risks, the chapter proposes a validation framework based on the concomitant variable model—the  coefficient test—to ensure that synthetic data preserves the joint mapping between covariates and preferences essential for effective market segmentation and targeting.

title: The Demand Factor in the Age of AI: Fiscal Principle, Measurement Architecture, and Financing Horizon
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Demand Factor in the Age of AI: Fiscal Principle, Measurement Architecture, and Financing Horizon
detail.abstract: This document is a conceptual and programmatic Discussion Paper, not a conventional academic article nor a closed technical proposal. Its purpose is to mark out a direction of research: to formulate an architecture for thinking about the relationship between artificial intelligence, effective demand, taxation, measurement, distribution, and financing. Formal propositions, quantitative calibration, rigorous modeling, legal codification, and empirical validation are deliberately beyond the scope of this text. They are not omitted because they are secondary, but because they belong to a later stage of the IRIS program-one that will require economists, jurists, public administrations, measurement specialists, AI experts, and technical experts capable of converting structural intuitions into verifiable designs. The contribution offered here is of a different kind: to order the problem, identify its levels, and propose categories capable of guiding further work. MAT, MAR, and MAD are presented as conceptual instruments and institutional directions. Their tax bases, rates, credits, thresholds, settlement procedures, appeal mechanisms, and forms of governance remain open to research, democratic deliberation, and institutional calibration. Any figures or orders of magnitude that appear in the text should be read as illustrative references. They are not definitive design parameters. They are intended to show the structural scale of the problem, not to close an implementation.

title: Generation–Verification Asymmetry Inversion and Apprenticeship Pipeline Collapse Under AI Substitution
affiliations: GenAI Architect; Independent Researcher

detail.title: Generation–Verification Asymmetry Inversion and Apprenticeship Pipeline Collapse Under AI Substitution

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is a theoretical contribution based exclusively on publicly available labor-economics statistics and standard published literature; it does not involve human participants, identifiable personal data, animal subjects, or any data requiring institutional ethics review.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The work was conducted by the author independently.

detail.abstract: For most of economic history, generation has been costly and verification cheap; tacit-capital institutions were optimized for that asymmetry. AI inverts the cost structure: generation becomes near-free while verification remains a Polanyi residual that is tacit and labor-intensive. We develop a tacit-capital production model with CES output in generation and verification, AI substitution at rate θ, and verification capacity acquired only through accumulated generation experience under h(τ)=τ^a. Two phenomena follow. The asymmetry inversion is a smooth equilibrium transition at θ_inv where the binding factor switches; markets handle it. The apprenticeship pipeline collapse is a phase transition at θ* = 1 − τ*/T_j where no cohort meets the promotion threshold; the steady-state verification stock undergoes a downward jump of ν T_s (τ*)^a and decays linearly to zero over the senior career length T_s with no market-mediated recovery. The credentialing return decays at rate a+b (Leontief) above θ* and at rate (1−η)(a+b) in Cobb-Douglas in the limit θ→1; both strictly exceed the pre-collapse rates. The apprenticeship externality gives a Pigouvian wedge non-decreasing on [0, θ*) for ρ ≤ 0 or ρ ∈ (0, 1/a) (under K_AI ≥ L_G), unbounded as θ→1 for ρ < 1/(a+b) in the smooth-threshold post-collapse regime, and collapsing to zero above θ* under hard promotion (g(ē) = 0). The wedge is distinct from a Lucas spillover because it grows endogenously in θ. Recursive verification shifts θ_inv leftward by ratio (K_AI − L_G)/(μK_AI − L_G), approaching 1/μ as K_AI → ∞, when AI output requires μ units of verification per unit of generation. A boundary proposition characterizes which professions collapse via the bundling share ζ_V of generation and verification within the productive act. Three adjustment margins (career extension, threshold reduction, endogenous AI verification) shift θ* rightward but cannot eliminate the collapse, since non-substitutability of the residual remains binding. Welfare aggregation shows that under near-Cobb-Douglas cross-profession aggregation (σ_a → 1) the least resilient profession sets the aggregate bottleneck; under gross complements (σ_a < 1) the collapsing profession dominates; in the intermediate regime (1 < σ_a < ∞) aggregate output remains positive after any single-profession collapse but the aggregate output decay rate is non-decreasing at each phase transition under Cobb-Douglas-within-profession with smooth promotion. Endogenous AI capacity yields a unique low-AI fixed point under monotonicity (Brouwer), with asymmetric hysteresis: the system can be pushed to the corner in finite time but recovery requires a full career length T = T_j + T_s. Quantitative calibration yields θ* ∈ {0.40, 0.20, 0.29} for software / radiology / law respectively, with collapse-onset ordering radiology → law → software, and lifetime Pigouvian per-junior subsidies in the range $1.55M–$3.21M under the Cobb-Douglas baseline (η = 0.5). The paper closes with five falsifiable predictions and three differentiated policy mechanisms. A companion Lean 4 / Mathlib machine-checked formalization is at https://github.com/crabsatellite/verification-asymmetry-lean4-formalization.

title: Premium Tea as the Third Regime 4 Datapoint: A Single-category Replication of the v0.13 Covariate-saturated weak Finding

detail.abstract:
Brand science distinguishes Mental Availability (memory salience) from Physical Availability (point-of-sale presence). The AIAS™ Measurement Programme introduces a third construct — AI Presence — operationalised as the rate at which each brand appears across matched LLM responses to category-recommendation prompts, and tests its construct validity against Google Trends rank as an external consumer-search proxy. v0.13 (five-category construct-validity expansion) identified a fourth empirical regime — Covariate-saturated weak (Regime 4) — in premium facial skincare and personal-finance apps. The regime was named provisionally pending a third independent replication.

v0.14 tests that replication in premium tea, a designed-for-test category selected for its highly fragmented brand landscape and the heavy weight of Asian-tradition specialty brands that English-language consumer search underrepresents. The pre-registered hypothesis H_Regime4_replication CONFIRMED at both measurement waves (t1 = 29 April 2026; t2 = 7 May 2026) and survives Tea Box-excluded sensitivity testing. All three pre-registered conditions hold at both waves: sample size n = 17 eligible brands worldwide (above the C1 floor of 12); bivariate Spearman rho(AI Presence × Google Trends) = -0.066 at t1 and -0.134 at t2 (within the C2 threshold |rho| < 0.35); partial rho after age + premium-tier control = -0.084 and -0.146 (satisfying C3 partial rho < 0). Tea Box-excluded sensitivity (n = 16) replicates: bivariate -0.011 / -0.129; partial -0.005 / -0.130.

Premium tea is the cleanest Regime 4 case observed in the programme to date. v0.13's skincare and finance both exhibited weakly positive bivariate rho that flipped to negative partial rho only after age and tier were controlled; premium tea bypasses that phase entirely, arriving at negative bivariate before any covariate adjustment. Three datapoints across three categories elevate Regime 4 from a provisional zone to a canonical pattern, and v0.14 evolves the headline classification axes from (bivariate rho × decrement) to (bivariate rho × partial rho) to accommodate categories with already-negative bivariate signal.

title: The Knowledge Structuring Model (KSM™): A Socio-Technical Framework for AI-Mediated Visibility and Citation Authority

detail.title: The Knowledge Structuring Model (KSM™): A Socio-Technical Framework for AI-Mediated Visibility and Citation Authority

detail.abstract: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is fundamentally reshaping the digital discovery landscape. Traditional search engine optimization (SEO)predicated on document retrieval, ranking, and link-based authority-is increasingly insufficient as user behavior shifts toward AI-mediated "answer engines" that synthesize information from distributed knowledge sources. In this emerging paradigm, visibility is no longer determined by page position but by an organization's inclusion and attribution within AI-generated responses. This paper introduces the Knowledge Structuring Model (KSM™), a theoretical and managerial framework for guiding the strategic transition from SEO to answer engine optimization (AEO) and generative engine optimization (GEO). Grounded in socio-technical systems theory and developed through a design science research (DSR) approach, KSM conceptualizes AI-mediated visibility as a function of three interdependent pillars: (1) extractable structured content, (2) entity salience and knowledge graph alignment, and (3) citation authority reinforcement. Drawing upon principles from semantic web technologies, information retrieval, and knowledge graph theory, the model advances a shift from document-centric optimization to entity-centric authority. The paper further proposes a governance model and measurement framework, addressing ethical considerations such as data accuracy and the privacy-visibility tradeoff. The study concludes with a structured roadmap and research agenda for organizations seeking to operationalize AI-native visibility in a post-search environment.

title: The Reset Premium: Option Value under Asymmetric Price Commitment
affiliations: University of Central Florida - College of Business Administration - Department of Economics and IMD

detail.title: The Reset Premium: Option Value under Asymmetric Price Commitment
detail.abstract: We show that a one-sided price-adjustment rule, with free price cuts but a fixed daily resetfor price increases, raises the reset price even under risk neutrality, mean-zero wholesalecost shocks, and perfect consumer information. The mechanism is option-theoretic:a higher reset price preserves pass-through in adverse cost states, while favorable shockscan still be accommodated by price cuts. In differentiated Bertrand competition, thereset premium scales with cost pass-through and hence with substitutability. The mechanismis distinct from consumer search and strategic price dispersion because it operateseven under perfect consumer price information.

detail.title: Unpacking Social Exposure

detail.abstract: We develop a method to measure firms' exposures to social issues from earningscall transcripts. The method applies large language models and decomposes social exposure into five domains: Employee Welfare, DEI, Stakeholder Outreach, Ethical Commitments, and Crisis Response. The measures cover over 15,000 firms across 93 countries from 2003 to 2024. The five domains exhibit distinct, sometimes opposing, associations with labor outcomes, productivity, and ESG ratings. Aggregating domains of differing sign attenuates estimated effects, consistent with the weak findings reported for composite social scores. Domains correlate with labor-market outcomes and productivity in different directions; the aggregate averages these correlations toward zero. Exploiting the Dobbs decision, which tightened abortion regulation, as a labor-supply shock, we find that firms with higher pre-Dobbs DEI exposure experienced a lower worker outflow than non-exposed firms in the same state and month.

title: The Radial Disruption Field: A Predictive Framework for Industrial Blast Radius Mapping

detail.title: The Radial Disruption Field: A Predictive Framework for Industrial Blast Radius Mapping
detail.abstract:
Most executives recognize a technology disruption after it has already hit their industry. By then, the displacement timeline is running and the window to respond is shrinking. This paper presents a framework for predicting which industries will be
displaced by a new technology, how severely, and when — before any displacement has occurred.

The Radial Disruption Field uses a single measurable property of each new technology — how much of its sub-technology stack it shares with adjacent industries — to calculate blast radius, field strength, and displacement timelines. Validated against seven disruptions spanning 1838 to 2022, the framework predicts industry displacement timing with a mean error under 1.5 years. A supplementary employment onset validation against BLS QCEW data for three completed disruptions produced an onset-based MAE of 0.00 years.

Three findings carry direct strategic weight. Industries showing revenue growth while losing market share have already entered the blast radius — revenue is a lagging indicator of disruption, not a leading one. A single disruption can arrive in
multiple waves years apart, each triggered by a specific capability threshold, meaning executives who survive the first wave face subsequent ones they may not have anticipated. And browser-native technologies deploy 40-60% faster than
older disruptions regardless of how mature their underlying components are, compressing the response window for AI-driven disruption to the shortest in the industrial record.

Applied prospectively to AI coding tools and Google Search, the framework produces specific displacement timelines by role and query type — and identifies a structural engineering talent gap that will peak in the mid-2030s as a second-order
consequence of current junior hiring collapse.

title: Artificial Intelligence in the Realm of Copyright Law: An Analytical Study
affiliations: Maharashtra National Law University , Nagpur

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence in the Realm of Copyright Law: An Analytical Study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA

detail.abstract: In the contemporary digital era, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a significant contributor to the creation of diverse creative works, ranging from literature and films to music and software. This paper delves into the intricate interplay between AI and Copyright Law, with a special emphasis on the Indian legal landscape. The study is rooted in the observation that the Indian copyright system, in its current form, struggles to accommodate the surge in AI-generated works. This predicament has given rise to widespread ambiguity regarding the copyright protection applicable to such works, not only within India but also on an international scale. The paper seeks to unravel this complexity by questioning the capacity of AI-generated works to fulfil the fundamental prerequisites of creative works as stipulated by copyright legislation. It further explores the intricate dynamics of authorship and ownership in the AI context, posing critical questions: can the AI or its programmer be deemed the author? Is it feasible to consider AI as a co-author or even accord it the status of legal personhood? Aiming to shed light on these issues, the research proposes potential solutions, drawing upon international norms and practices adopted by developed nations such as the European Union, the United States of America and Japan. In conclusion, this paper aspires to enrich the discourse on AI and copyright law, offering valuable insights that could guide lawmakers, practitioners, and scholars in navigating this complex intersection.

title: Legal Deserts Over Time
affiliations: University of Kentucky - J. David Rosenberg College of Law

detail.title: Legal Deserts Over Time
detail.abstract:
Legal deserts—counties with exceptionally low attorney availability—shape housing stability, personal safety, health outcomes, and economic security in rural communities.  Yet, national scholarship has not yet determined whether attorney scarcity is transient or durable and relies largely on cross-sectional snapshots and population-based headcounts benchmarked to the American Bar Association’s (ABA) threshold of one attorney per 1,000 residents.  These measures can obscure temporal dynamics, overstate functional supply, and embed contested normative assumptions about adequacy.

This Article offers a national, longitudinal, and definition-sensitive analysis of legal deserts using county-level data from the forty-eight contiguous states at three observation points.  Attorney supply is measured using employment-based data from the U.S. Census Bureau’s County Business Patterns and assessed using both the ABA benchmark and an emerging, demand-adjusted threshold of 0.5 attorneys per 1,000 residents, alongside attorney gap measures calibrated to the rural-urban context. The analysis further situates attorney scarcity within place-based structural conditions by examining variation across rurality, Appalachian Regional Commission counties, and persistent poverty counties.

Across both definitions, legal deserts are overwhelmingly persistent.  Counties rarely exited desert status over the eight-year observation period, and entry more often reflected sustained erosion.  How a legal desert is defined materially alters the picture of scarcity: the ABA definition identifies a larger, more margin-sensitive set of counties with greater apparent movement, while the demand-adjusted threshold isolates a smaller but more entrenched set facing severe shortages.  Legal deserts cluster in geographically isolated counties and are disproportionately concentrated in Appalachian and persistent poverty counties, where long-term economic distress compounds rural disadvantage.  Proximity to metropolitan areas often substitutes for, rather than rebuilds, locally embedded legal capacity.  Together, these findings recast legal deserts as a durable infrastructure deficit and suggest that access-to-justice policy should be evaluated by whether it restores stable local capacity over time.

title: Key contractual factors influencing safety practices on construction sites
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Key contractual factors influencing safety practices on construction sites
detail.abstract: Occupational safety and health (OSH) problems remain prevalent in the construction industry. Previous research has emphasized on-site hazards, fragmented project organization, and client engagement, but less is known about how contractual arrangements shape safety practices during the construction phase. This paper examines which contractual factors enable good safety practices in construction projects.,The empirical foundation for the study is 17 construction projects, combining assessments of tender and contract documents with ethnographic fieldwork on active construction sites. Contractual conditions and observed safety practices were analyzed using Coincidence Analysis and interpreted through qualitative case vignettes.,The analysis identifies three pathways to strong safety round practices, which in turn co-occurred with higher scores on safety practice on site. 1) high-quality contract material combined with explicit descriptions of OSH methods reduced ambiguity and supported routine preventive work. 2) explicit OSH methods were effective when connected to a hierarchy-of-controls logic that directed attention toward elimination, substitution, and higher-order risk controls. 3) systematic OSH management descriptions, including clear roles, meeting structures, feedback loops, and coordinator mandates, could independently support effective safety rounds. Case vignettes illustrate how these contractual configurations were enacted in practice, and how weak contract descriptions were associated with more ad hoc safety work.,The study shows how contracts and plans for health and safety (PHS) can function as upstream organizational devices shaping practical safety coordination. The findings suggest that clients and OSH professionals can strengthen construction-phase safety by specifying OSH methods, applying hierarchy-of-controls thinking, and embedding safety rounds within systematic management.

title: Mandatory ESG Disclosure and Corporate Green Innovation: Evidence from the Hong Kong Exchange's 2020 Policy Upgrade
affiliations: Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation (CAITEC)

detail.title: Mandatory ESG Disclosure and Corporate Green Innovation: Evidence from the Hong Kong Exchange's 2020 Policy Upgrade
detail.abstract: We examine whether mandatory ESG disclosure is associated with changes in corporate green innovation, using the Hong Kong Exchange's 2020 policy upgrade as a quasi-natural experiment. In a matched panel of 153 Chinese firms (2012-2023) with A+H cross-listed firms as the treatment group, green patent grants show a positive estimate at lag 2 (adjusted p = 0.042 after core-family Bonferroni correction). Application-side estimates are positive at lag 1 (adjusted p = 0.068), directional but above the 5% threshold. The distributed lag model confirms application effects concentrate at lag 1 and grant effects at lag 2, consistent with patent examination cycles. The response is concentrated in invention patents without quality-proxy improvement. Standard transmission channels produce null results. Under full-family Bonferroni correction (21 tests), no result passes 5%. These findings point to a directional quantity response without quality improvement, extending the quantity-quality divergence literature to mandatory disclosure.

detail.abstract: This paper documents empirical patterns consistent with fiscal dominance by coordination in Indonesia's 2020-2024 burden-sharing episode. Using a smoothingaugmented Taylor rule estimated via GMM-IV, we find that Bank Indonesia's long-run inflation responsiveness declines from 0.955 under low fiscal stress to 0.420 under high stress. The findings suggest that quasi-fiscal coordination without institutional safeguards can attenuate monetary policy space in emerging markets.

affiliations: Chongqing University - School of Economics and Business Admininstration

detail.title: Token Budgets as Incentive Instruments
detail.abstract: We study when and how generously firms should subsidize AI access through token budgets. A firm hires a worker who allocates AI use between productive experimentation and private "gaming." A larger budget lowers the worker's marginal cost of AI use, making experimentation cheaper to induce, but shifts token spending to the firm and potentially subsidizes gaming. Absent gaming, uncapped access is optimal: the firm fully finances AI use to minimize incentive payments. When gaming is possible, finite or zero budgets can be optimal as disciplinary devices; yet uncapped access remains optimal if high experimentation crowds out gaming. In competitive labor markets, token budgets can support first-best equilibria that a zero budget cannot. Stronger competition can tighten access limits, while higher token prices may relax them. Token budgets are therefore best understood not merely as tools for talent attraction or cost control, but as incentive instruments.
