Limitations of perception-based measurement, convenience sampling, and the absence of objective performance outcomes as dependent variables are explicitly acknowledged. This study makes two contributions: it maps the decision-making infrastructure of experienced SEZ actors-the shared mental model that governs how zones are built, regulated, and invested in worldwide-and it provides the variable prioritisation framework that future causal research will require to test which conditions actually drive zone performance. The study is explicitly designed as Stage 1 of a two-stage research programme; Stage 2, linking these variables to objective zone-level outcomes, is the logical and necessary next step.

title: Evaluation Is Not Judgment, Nor Assessment: A Tri-layer Cognitive Framework Explaining the Failure of Rationality and the Puzzles of Behavioral Economics
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Evaluation Is Not Judgment, Nor Assessment: A Tri-layer Cognitive Framework Explaining the Failure of Rationality and the Puzzles of Behavioral Economics

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study involved minimal‑risk behavioral tasks with adult participants, using non‑sensitive self‑reported judgments and previously completed online purchases. No personal identifying information or sensitive data were collected. According to standard institutional guidelines for exempt research, formal ethics committee approval was not required. All participants provided informed consent prior to participation.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
This study proposes a revised Tri-Layer Cognitive Architecture grounded in a two-tier structural division: a temporal partition between pre-behavioral and post-behavioral processing, and a functional distinction within pre-behavioral cognition. Human decisionmaking is divided into two independent temporal stages: pre-behavioral Judgment and post-behavioral Assessment. Within pre-behavioral cognition, Evaluation (E) and Judgment (J) are defined as two distinct constructs, with Evaluation serving as an independent input dimension of Judgment rather than an embedded sub-unit. Judgment is a constrained decision output jointly determined by Evaluation, explicit price, and other external constraints, formulated as 𝐽 = 𝑓(𝐸, 𝑃𝑟𝑖𝑐𝑒, 𝑂𝑡ℎ𝑒𝑟𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑡𝑟𝑎𝑖𝑛𝑡𝑠). Post-behavioral Assessment (A) functions as a temporally independent retrospective evaluation that may deviate from both E and J. 
Mainstream behavioral economics and psychological research conventionally regard human cognition as a unified continuum, assuming equivalence among preference, decision and post-choice evaluation. This monolithic view fails to explain persistent theoretical puzzles including the attitude-behavior gap, unstable willingness to pay, preference reversal, and bounded rationality. This paper conducts a structural test of the three-layer framework via an online apparel consumption experiment with high ecological validity. The results indicate that: (1) Evaluation is a stable, deliberate pure value judgment independent of behavioral intention and price; (2) constrained monetary Judgment cannot converge to a single-point threshold and naturally forms a vague interval even with clear Evaluation; (3) post-behavioral Assessment deviates substantially from prior Evaluation, with 85% of participants showing attitudinal fluctuation or reversal. 
The findings empirically confirm the functional separation of Evaluation and Judgment, the temporal independence of Assessment, and asynchronous evolution within the overall cognitive architecture. The framework offers a unified structural account of behavioral anomalies and provides a new theoretical foundation for preference measurement, pricing decisions and post-choice evaluation in behavioral economics and cognitive psychology.

title: Measuring Contagion Risk in Botswana’s Financial System
affiliations: Bank of Botswana and  Bank of Botswana

detail.title: Measuring Contagion Risk in Botswana’s Financial System

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We have no relationships to declare with regard to this research.
declarations.funderStatement: Research was not funded by any third party. Although the authors are employees of the Bank of Botswana, the views expressed in this paper are solely those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the official position of the Bank.

detail.abstract: This paper applies centrality measures, a systemic risk measure and DebtRank index to compute contagion indices for the Botswana financial system. Using March 2024 data, we reveal that the banking sector drives activity in the domestic financial system, both as a direct intermediary and indirectly through interlinkages that transfer information and funds across the financial system. Overall, the domestic financial system is highly interconnected and negative externalities can easily propagate, with broader financial stability implications. The study thus strengthens the supervisory oversight for systemic risks, thereby enhancing the domestic macroprudential surveillance.

title: Role of Entrepreneurial Universities, Research Centers and Economic Zones in Driving Entrepreneurship and Innovation in Cluster Ecosystems
affiliations: Maalexi Inc.

detail.title: Role of Entrepreneurial Universities, Research Centers and Economic Zones in Driving Entrepreneurship and Innovation in Cluster Ecosystems
detail.abstract: Economic zones are recognized as contributors of entrepreneurship and innovation and key elements of national development strategy. This paper empirically evaluates and answers questions like - is there an impact of entrepreneurial universities and research centers on the performance of clusters? why and how this happens? do economic zones affect cluster outputs to the host economy? can there be enhancement of entrepreneurship and innovation in clusters if economic zones are bundled along with entrepreneurial universities and research centers? This study builds up on the dataset of top-100 clusters of innovation, presented by World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), refining it and adding five socio-economic output indicators, testing for three independent variables (entrepreneurial universities, research centers and economic zones) to reveal, quantify the relationships and evaluate the impact of these variables on cluster performance. The results show there is a strong effect of all three independent variables but with varying degrees on different socio-economic output indicators, implying that a hybrid or collaborative mod-el with entrepreneurial universities, research centers and economic zones will be the most emphatic alliance to deliver the socio-economic benefits expected out of the clusters.

title: Djibouti: A Hub for Expanding Islamic Finance Across ‘Horn of Africa’
affiliations: Maalexi Inc.

detail.title: Djibouti: A Hub for Expanding Islamic Finance Across ‘Horn of Africa’
detail.abstract: Islamic Finance is a growing rapidly across Africa, where around 40% of the population is Muslims and is now offered across 21 African countries, with one country leading the pack – Djibouti. Djibouti can be referred as ‘logistical and financial hub for East Africa’ due to its fast-growing port access and availability, progressive banking regulations and strong intra-regional connectivity with Ethiopia and other landlocked countries which have no or poor port access. Besides logistics, other sectors that continue to show significant growth in Djibouti include banking and financial services, tourism, and hospitality, education and telecommunications. This article presents the status of Islamic finance in Djibouti, challenges it faces and its future in the region.

title: Speaking Fast and Low: The Acoustics of Authoritarian Politics
affiliations: and The Hebrew University of Jerusalem - Department of Economics

detail.title: Speaking Fast and Low: The Acoustics of Authoritarian Politics

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: The authors acknowledge financing from King's College London

detail.abstract: Do political regimes shape how citizens speak? Exploiting a large audio corpus, we compare the voice of Mandarin speakers from Mainland China (an authoritarian regime) vs Taiwan (a democracy) reading randomly assigned sentences. We find that, compared to Taiwanese, mainland Chinese men speak "fast and low" about political content: with about 0.2 SD higher tempo and 0.4 SD lower volume, consistent with low-arousal fear in Mandarin phonetics. Mirroring the gendered pattern of political repression, we find no comparable effect among women. Historical repression amplifies these patterns: within China, tempo is faster in provinces with higher Cultural Revolution fatalities, but not in those more repressed today. Citizens' daily speech can reveal the institutional setting they live under, with normative and methodological implications for the study of self-censorship, deliberation, and data collection under authoritarian rule.

title: Three Decades of Euribor: Viability and Prospects for Future Development
affiliations: Comisión Nacional del Mercado de Valores (CNMV), BBVA and Comisión Nacional del Mercado de Valores (CNMV)

detail.title: Three Decades of Euribor: Viability and Prospects for Future Development
detail.abstract: This paper analyses the evolution and current role of Euribor as a key benchmark of the European financial system following the international reform of financial benchmarks. By examining its governance, methodology, representativeness and interaction with risk-free rates based on the €STR, the analysis shows that Euribor retains a distinct economic role as a forward-looking benchmark incorporating bank credit risk, which remains particularly relevant for retail lending and for contracts with long remaining maturities. The paper identifies as the main lines of future development a potential deeper reliance on eligible transaction-based data from the ECB’s MMSR, a strengthening of public supervisory arrangements relative to audit-intensive private oversight models, and the adoption of solutions aimed at enhancing the efficiency and long-term viability of the benchmark, without undermining its continuity or systemic function, in line with the European regulatory framework and financial stability objectives.

title:
Stabilizing the Conditions of Transition   
A Field-Based Systems Analysis of Workforce Readiness and Structural Alignment

detail.title:
Stabilizing the Conditions of Transition   
A Field-Based Systems Analysis of Workforce Readiness and Structural Alignment
detail.abstract:
Workforce readiness systems have historically emphasized access-based models centered on placement, participation, and exposure to authentic work environments. However, persistent instability in engagement, regulation, persistence, and task completion suggests that access alone is insufficient to produce sustainable workforce outcomes for students with disabilities and other vulnerable populations.

This field-based implementation study examines workforce readiness through the emerging discipline of Human-Centered Systems Design, developed through The Starlings Institute. Human-Centered Systems Design studies how systems produce outcomes-and how environmental, relational, instructional, and structural conditions determine whether those outcomes stabilize or fragment over time. Within this discipline, Educational Architecture functions as the initial applied domain focused specifically on learning, development, regulation, and workforce readiness environments. 

Using a phased comparative implementation within a transition-aligned workforce readiness system, this study examined two system conditions: 
1. Community-based workforce placement without coordinated structural alignment 
2. Placement combined with aligned vocational instruction, integrated supports, adult coordination, and applied learning environments

Findings demonstrate that placement alone increased exposure and short-term engagement but failed to produce stable improvements in regulation, persistence, or workforce performance. Significant improvements emerged only when learner conditions and structural systems became aligned and coherent.

The study operationalizes Human Conditions Theory through the Human Conditions Index (HCI) and Coherence Index (CI), creating a dual-framework measurement model for assessing learner condition stability and structural alignment across workforce systems.

Findings suggest that workforce readiness outcomes are not produced primarily by programs or interventions, but by the stabilization and alignment of the conditions surrounding the learner.

title: Team Gender Composition and Firm Performance: Experimental Evidence from Solar Entrepreneurs in Rwanda
affiliations: , Duke University, Fuqua School of Business, Universidad del Pacifico and University of Cape Town - Faculty of Commerce - School of Economics

detail.title: Team Gender Composition and Firm Performance: Experimental Evidence from Solar Entrepreneurs in Rwanda
detail.abstract: How does team gender composition affect the performance of small technology-enabled firms in the Global South? We study this question using a field experiment with 270 village-level solar enterprises in rural Rwanda, where teams of four entrepreneurs were randomly assigned to be all-male, all-female, or mixed-gender. Over 18 months, mixed-gender teams underperform all-male teams by approximately 40%, while all-female teams also underperform all-male teams by 24%, with point estimates placing all-female teams between the all-male and mixed arms. To probe mechanisms, we pair the 18-month administrative output data with minute-level GSM timestamp data over the first six months. Mixed teams generate fewer recharges during evening peak-demand hours, while all-female teams do not exhibit the peak-hour coordination deficit. Despite lower business revenues, all-female teams generate distinctive household-level spillovers, with children studying approximately 74 additional minutes per week. Our findings suggest that performance in small entrepreneurial firms depends critically on whether teams can organize around conflicting and often binding temporal constraints.

title: Do lenders price diesel risk? Evidence from Dieselgate and low-emission zones in captive vs. independent banks
affiliations: Leibniz Institute for Financial Research SAFE, European Central Bank (ECB), University of Zurich - Department Finance and KU Leuven, Department Accounting, Finance and Insurance

detail.title: Do lenders price diesel risk? Evidence from Dieselgate and low-emission zones in captive vs. independent banks
detail.abstract: Transitioning to a sustainable economy and reducing air pollution hinge on appropriate economic incentives and financing conditions. The auto loan market offers a prime setting, as lenders’ credit terms can either discourage or incentivize the purchase of high-pollution vehicles. Using loan-level data, we examine how captive and independent banks adjust lending conditions in response to information and regulatory shocks affecting diesel vehicles. Exploiting the 2015 diesel emissions scandal and the introduction of local circulation restrictions, we show that lending responses differ systematically across lender types, with captive banks tending to weaken, rather than reinforce, the effectiveness of environmental regulation for air pollution.

title: Buying Brains with M&A: Talent Reallocation, Labor Market Power and Firm Boundaries
affiliations: Toulouse Business School,  and CREST-Ensai

detail.title: Buying Brains with M&A: Talent Reallocation, Labor Market Power and Firm Boundaries
detail.abstract: This paper studies how mergers and acquisitions affect talent reallocation, labor market power and firm boundaries. Using matched firm-worker data from LinkedIn and antitrust-screened M&A events, we show that an completed M&A is followed by higher skilled talent inflows into the acquirer, lower wages for acquirer's workers and more bonus losses for executives absorbed from targets. Firms also expand their boundaries after M&A. We rationalize these findings with a model in which the target privately observes its workers' abilities. Before the merger, the target bids up wages for high-ability workers through counteroffers; after the merger, the acquirer inherits this information and the target disappears as an informed competitor, making talent acquisition cheaper. An extension allowing information leakage to outside employers attenuates the wage-suppression effect.

title: ECB exchange rate communication
affiliations: European Stability Mechanism, , European Central Bank (ECB), European Central Bank (ECB) and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: ECB exchange rate communication
detail.abstract: We revisit the debate on the effectiveness of central bank communication on exchange rates, contrasting a skeptical view, which holds that communication neither moves exchange rates nor influences them in the desired direction, with an optimistic view that it does. Using nearly 100 official ECB statements on exchange rates made during its monetary policy press conferences since 2002, we show that the ECB tends to mention the exchange rate when the real effective exchange rate deviates from its equilibrium value, whereas journalists’ questions are mainly responsive to the nominal exchange rate. Studying the effects of these mentions, our findings by and large support the skeptical view: after controlling for monetary policy shocks, exchange rate communication has limited immediate effects on the euro exchange rate, which fade quickly. Effectiveness is particularly limited when interest rates are at their effective lower bound.

title: Supply chain uncertainty, energy prices, and inflation
affiliations: and Bocconi University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Supply chain uncertainty, energy prices, and inflation
detail.abstract: Using U.S. and Euro area data, we document that (i) the pass-through of energy prices to inflation is state-dependent - stronger when supply chain uncertainty is elevated – and (ii) in such states, energy prices become more informative about logistical conditions. We develop a model in which firms combine energy and a specialized input transported through a capacity-constrained transportation network. When congestion binds, energy remains available in local markets at a premium, whereas the specialized input is subject to delivery delays. Because energy prices reflect both raw energy shocks and transportation conditions, firms treat them as noisy signals of supply disruptions and update beliefs through Bayesian learning. This signal-extraction channel increases perceived marginal costs, generating an uncertainty wedge that amplifies and propagates energy shocks. Within a general-equilibrium New Keynesian model, the mechanism raises the impact elasticity and the persistence of inflation in response to transitory energy shocks. This challenges the conventional monetary policy prescription to “look through” supply disturbances.

title: Wildfire cashflow shocks
affiliations: and University of Porto, Faculty of Economics

detail.title: Wildfire cashflow shocks
detail.abstract: This paper studies the impact on cashflows and financial decisions of firms affected by wildfires, focusing on the wildfires that occurred in Portugal in 2017. Using establishment-level data from the hotel industry combined with geospatial information on wildfire proximity and land use, we employ a difference-in-differences approach to study both directly and indirectly affected firms. Our findings reveal that firms with direct damages from the wildfires recorded, on average, a 43% drop in revenues in 2018, while indirectly affected firms with a high share of burned area within a 1 km radius suffered a 24% drop. These cashflow shocks triggered distinct financial responses: directly affected hotels increased their reliance on long-term debt and coupled tangible asset investments with additional cash reserves, whereas indirectly affected firms reduced tangible investments and cash holdings. This divergence aligns with both real-options and reference-dependent risk preferences theories, reflecting the option to wait before investing and the shift in business fundamentals relative to the pre-disaster reference points.

title: Buying Brains with M&A: Talent Reallocation, Labor Market Power and Firm Boundaries
affiliations: CREST-Ensai,  and Toulouse Business School

detail.title: Buying Brains with M&A: Talent Reallocation, Labor Market Power and Firm Boundaries
detail.abstract: This paper studies how mergers and acquisitions affect talent reallocation, labor market power and firm boundaries. Using matched firm-worker data from LinkedIn and antitrust-screened M&A events, we show that an completed M&A is followed by higher skilled talent inflows into the acquirer, lower wages for acquirer's workers and more bonus losses for executives absorbed from targets. Firms also expand their boundaries after M&A. We rationalize these findings with a model in which the target privately observes its workers' abilities. Before the merger, the target bids up wages for high-ability workers through counteroffers; after the merger, the acquirer inherits this information and the target disappears as an informed competitor, making talent acquisition cheaper. An extension allowing information leakage to outside employers attenuates the wage-suppression effect.

title: Affinities between Different Entrepreneurial Ecosystems and Economic Zones
affiliations: Maalexi Inc.

detail.title: Affinities between Different Entrepreneurial Ecosystems and Economic Zones
detail.abstract: Entrepreneurial ecosystems can take different forms, some of the conspicuous ones are country, city, cluster and economic zone. All these four entrepreneurial ecosystems are based on certain variables which affect their characteristics, performance, and impact. The models for evaluating entrepreneurial ecosystems based in a country, city, and a cluster are well established but there is no standardized and empirical model to evaluate economic zone based entrepreneurial ecosystems. In this paper, a methodology is adopted and re-designed to evaluate the relationships or affinities between the four types of entrepreneurial ecosystems. This study lays the theoretical foundation for a comprehensive empirical study for analyzing economic zone entrepreneurial ecosystems, based on the proposed model, for gaining insight and direction on how to create and optimize economic zone as instruments of national competitive advantage. The key questions that are discussed in this study are – why are entrepreneurial ecosystems relevant? what are the variables that drive entrepreneurial ecosystems? which model can be applied to assess affinities between four selected entrepreneurial ecosystem types? what learnings from study of these affinities can be applied to develop economic zone based entrepreneurial ecosystems? The results show a positive correlation between economic zone and cluster and city, based on data from WEF survey on entrepreneurial ecosystems collected on 8-pillars and 38 sub-variables, through responses from 1000 entrepreneurs across 49countries. The results provide a basis to foster advanced research in understanding and experimenting with economic zone based entrepreneurial ecosystems, and re-designing and deploying already existing models for evaluating economic zones.

title: Existence and Relevance of Economic Zones - A Strategic Development Perspective
affiliations: Maalexi Inc.

detail.title: Existence and Relevance of Economic Zones - A Strategic Development Perspective
detail.abstract: In this paper, economic zones have been evaluated through descriptive analysis, and the context of their existence and relevance is substantiated by theoretical reasoning. A classification model and critical dimensions for evaluation were developed and deployed to gather and analyze data on economic zones. An exhaustive exercise was undertaken for identifying, collecting, consolidating, and analyzing data on economic zones, which provided insight into the existence of 3,588 economic zones geographically spread across 141 countries classified into 13 economic zone types. Comparisons on eight external and internal factors that affect zone presence have been thoroughly undertaken to discern the strategic development of the national policy of different countries for utilizing economic zones as tools for socio-economic development. The results provide a rationale for the relevance of economic zones by establishing relationships between country context, and economic zone taxonomic data. One of the important conclusions of this research is that majority of economic zones are based in factor-based countries, involved with low to medium-innovation industries, but are gradually either evolving or diverging into clusters; and continue to be a crucial tool for 'dynamic national socio-economic development' program in developing countries. A significant portion of countries have been unable to use economic zones as tools for industrial development and up-gradation, except UAE which has derived significant benefits in totality through zones, other countries that can further enhance the output of their zones include the Philippines, Vietnam, India, US, China, Thailand, Columbia, Indonesia, and Kenya. This research is the first step to undertake comprehensive studies into evaluating variables that drive, and outcomes that are delivered through the economic zones.

title: Finite Element Simulation Driven Reduced-Order Operator Learning Method for Parabolic Equations and Navier-Stokes Equations
affiliations: Sichuan University

detail.title: Finite Element Simulation Driven Reduced-Order Operator Learning Method for Parabolic Equations and Navier-Stokes Equations
detail.abstract: This work presents a reduced-order operator learning methodology for \emph{transient} (time-dependent) parameterized PDEs that combines Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) with Partially Input Convex Neural Networks (PICNN). The central objective is to learn the \emph{reduced internal force operator}\begin{equation*}\mathcal{F}_r^{\mathrm{int}}: \R^n \times \R^p \to \R^n, \quad (\bm{q}, \bm{\mu}) \mapsto \bm{f}_r^{\text{int}}(\bm{q}; \bm{\mu}),\end{equation*}where $n$ is the reduced dimension (number of retained POD modes), $p$ is the number of parameters, and $\bm{f}_r^{\text{int}}(\bm{q}; \bm{\mu}) \in \R^n$ is the reduced internal force vector that appears in the reduced ODE, i.e., the Galerkin projection of the full-order internal force. The learned surrogate for $\mathcal{F}_r^{\mathrm{int}}$ is evaluated at \emph{each time level} $t_j = j\Delta t$ ($j = 0, 1, \ldots, N_t$) during online time integration to advance the reduced solution from $\bm{q}^j$ to $\bm{q}^{j+1}$, so that the ROM can reproduce the transient evolution at arbitrary time instants. The approach constructs a low-dimensional representation of the solution manifold through POD from snapshots at discrete time levels and employs a physics-augmented neural network to approximate the reduced operator from high-fidelity simulation data. The PICNN architecture enforces convexity with respect to the reduced coordinates, providing inherent stability guarantees that standard neural networks lack. The framework treats the full-order model as a data generator, extracting the operator structure without requiring access to system matrices or assembly routines. We demonstrate the methodology on linear parabolic equations, the nonlinear incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, and Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes equations with k-$\varepsilon$ turbulence closure, presenting a unified treatment that addresses the distinct challenges posed by each problem class. Numerical experiments validate the accuracy and efficiency of the approach, achieving mean relative errors below 1\% and sub-percent relative errors in most cases, while providing significant computational speedups in the online phase.

reference: forthcoming in Journal of International Accounting, Auditing and Taxation
title: Dividend-Withholding Taxes, Income Shifting, and the Location of Intermediate Subsidiaries
affiliations: Vienna University of Economics and Business and University of Graz

detail.title: Dividend-Withholding Taxes, Income Shifting, and the Location of Intermediate Subsidiaries

publicationDetails.detailsText: forthcoming in Journal of International Accounting, Auditing and Taxation

detail.abstract: We examine how tax incentives influence the location choice for intermediate subsidiaries, namely entities that hold ownership stakes in foreign terminal subsidiaries. Using a global sample of multinational corporations (MNCs) with the option to locate subsidiaries across 37 European countries, we find that higher tax costs associated with dividend repatriation, particularly dividend-withholding taxes, significantly reduce the likelihood that a country is chosen as a location for an intermediate subsidiary. Cross-sectional analyses reveal that this effect is moderated by MNCs' income shifting opportunities and incentives. Specifically, the impact of dividend-withholding taxes varies depending on whether income shifting and dividend repatriation act as substitutes or complements in reallocating profits within MNCs. Overall, our findings deepen the understanding of tax-driven locational decisions for intermediate subsidiaries and highlight the conditions under which tax incentives affect a country's attractiveness as a subsidiary location.

title: Probabilistic modeling of extraordinary loads in buildings using big data-driven stochastic simulation: Methodology, applications, and extreme value analysis
affiliations: Tongji University, Tongji University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Tongji University and Tongji University

detail.title: Probabilistic modeling of extraordinary loads in buildings using big data-driven stochastic simulation: Methodology, applications, and extreme value analysis
detail.abstract: Extraordinary loads in building structures are characterized by short durations, low occurrence frequencies and large variability in load amplitudes, which introduce significant uncertainty into their stochastic evolution. Traditional survey methods relying on subjective human memory inevitably introduce significant epistemic uncertainties. To overcome these inherent limitations, this study proposes a robust stochastic simulation framework driven by big data for the objective probabilistic modeling of extraordinary loads. By synergizing virtual reality (VR) property systems with physical furniture databases scraped from e-commerce platforms, Monte Carlo simulations are executed strictly according to the physical significance of two primary transient events, specifically temporary furniture stacking and crowd gatherings, to generate representative load amplitude samples with high fidelity. Furthermore, a global sensitivity analysis based on Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence indicates that the extreme value distribution of the maximum combined load is predominantly governed by the variability of load amplitudes, whereas the influence of occurrence intervals is negligible. Based on this finding, the compound Poisson point process is reduced to a stationary binomial process, providing an efficient approach for structural reliability assessment.

title: When ambiguity reveals implicit preferences: A willingness to pay experiment on sustainable demand
affiliations: University of Bern, Agroscope, University of Bern and Agroscope

detail.title: When ambiguity reveals implicit preferences: A willingness to pay experiment on sustainable demand
detail.abstract: Individuals frequently express moral and pro-environmental preferences that are not reflected in their actual behavior. Understanding why people do not “walk their talk” is a central question in behavioral economics. One explanation is that while explicitly stating preferences for more sustainable products due to signaling motives, many individuals hold implicit preferences for conventional alternatives. Ambiguous decision contexts offer individuals excuses that make such hidden preferences easier to express. We test this mechanism in the domain of sustainable food by applying a novel framework for identifying implicit preferences (Cunningham & de Quidt, 2024) and by experimentally varying social exposure. In an incentivized laboratory experiment, participants repeatedly indicated their willingness to pay (WTP) for conventional and organic eggs under varying levels of ambiguity induced by an additional, unrelated product attribute. According to the framework, ambiguity dilutes reasoning and increases the likelihood of revealing implicit preferences. Consistent with this prediction, increased ambiguity led participants to reveal higher WTP for conventional eggs. However, only participants with strong social image concerns lowered their WTP for organic eggs when the reasoning was diluted.

title: The role of biodiversity risk in shaping bank lending decisions
affiliations: and

detail.title: The role of biodiversity risk in shaping bank lending decisions
detail.abstract: We examine whether banks incorporate firm-level biodiversity risk into their lending decisions. Using a large sample of syndicated loans matched to firm-level biodiversity risk measures, we document that borrowers with higher biodiversity risk face significantly higher loan spreads. Evidence on loan volumes is weaker, suggesting that banks primarily adjust along the pricing margin rather than restricting credit supply. To capture biodiversity risk exposure, we develop a novel text-based indicator derived from corporate disclosures that incorporates the contextual content of environmental risk. To strengthen identification, we exploit firm-level environmental violations as shocks to environmental credibility. In a stacked difference-in-differences framework, we show that such violations increase the sensitivity of loan pricing to biodiversity risk. Overall, our findings provide evidence that biodiversity risk is a financially material dimension of environmental risk in credit markets.

title: Legal Status and Parenthood: The Role of the 2002 Italian Regularization Reform
affiliations: University of Perugia, University of Perugia, University of Perugia and Catholic University of Rome

detail.title: Legal Status and Parenthood: The Role of the 2002 Italian Regularization Reform
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the effect of Italy's 2002 regularization law on immigrant women's fertility behavior, leveraging plausibly exogenous variation in the number of regularized immigrants employed in domestic work and industry. Using the 2002 and 2005 waves of the Birth Sample Survey (BSS), we show that regularized immigrant women experienced a statistically significant increase in the probability of having a first child following the change in their legal and employment status. By focusing on first births rather than completed fertility, the paper identifies the short-run extensive-margin effect of legal status on entry into motherhood, relative to both immigrants who had acquired Italian citizenship and Italian mothers, potentially accounting for roughly one-third of the increase in first births among immigrant women during the regularization period.Instead, we find no statistically significant effect on second or higher-order births. Our analysis reveals that the positive effect on first births is primarily driven by a reduction in uncertainty, a benefit that also extends to women with a documented partner. Moreover, legal status improves access to health care and lowers the incidence of induced abortion. Overall, these findings highlight the central role of legal status in promoting social integration and enabling immigrant women to embark on family formation.

title: Incorporating human factors into bicycle microscopic simulation: Methods and applications for modelling cycling capability
affiliations: Zhejiang Police College, Tongji University, Southwest Jiaotong University, Tongji University, Zhejiang Police College, Zhejiang Police College and Tongji University

detail.title: Incorporating human factors into bicycle microscopic simulation: Methods and applications for modelling cycling capability
detail.abstract: Incorporation of more sophisticated human factors (HFs) into microscopic traffic simulation has become a mainstream research direction in recent years. Such models are believed to enable us to further improve the performance of simulation, and to understand the mechanisms behind many puzzling traffic phenomena. In this regard, it can not only provide more accurate traffic flow estimation for management and facility design, but also support the development of autonomous driving by providing more realistic virtual testing simulation environments in traffic. Although related discussions and models for the operational behaviour of drivers and pedestrians are already extensive, studies on incorporating HFs into microscopic simulation models of cyclists are still nascent. Most existing research still focuses on how different types, genders, and cycling styles affect interaction behaviour, and captures such characteristics by distinguishing values of model parameters. Solutions for endogenously representing and depicting human cycling behaviours remain very limited. This limitation brings bicycle simulation models’ inability in accurately capturing heterogeneous human cycling behaviours and the variation of interaction states generated by HFs, resulting in unsatisfactory simulation performance. To this end, we attempt to incorporate HFs into bicycle behaviour models to address this gap. In this paper, we first select a key HF, i.e., cycling capability, as the modelling attribute of cyclist, and accordingly propose a novel cycling “Demand-Capability” framework to endogenously quantify the influence of this HF attribute on cyclist interactions. Corresponding formulations are developed, and testing is carefully designed for the model validation. Then, we further integrate the above model into our previously developed two‑dimensional bicycle simulation model. Here, two dedicated approaches are correspondingly put forward to address the effects of HFs on the operational mental (decision) and operational physical (action) activities, respectively. Finally, we perform face validation of the proposed simulation model by comparing simulation results with observations obtained from the empirical trajectory dataset. Results show the proposed model outperforms its predecessors, especially in the presence of individual behaviour decisions and actions.

title: The role of judgement in supervisory scores and additional capital requirements assigned to banks
affiliations: and

detail.title: The role of judgement in supervisory scores and additional capital requirements assigned to banks
detail.abstract: We empirically analyse the role of judgement in assigning overall scores by the euro area supervisors as part of the yearly Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process (SREP), which evaluates banks’ risks and sets supervisory actions. We also analyse its role in shaping the drivers of the Pillar 2 capital requirement (P2R) that banks must fulfil. We find that supervisors actively adjust the weight of the components of the overall score to reflect qualitative information, thereby smoothing fluctuations in the final assessment. The analysis reveals a common supervisory judgement channel, which could reflect shared priorities and concerns, such as systemic vulnerabilities or macroeconomic conditions. We also show that certain risks, such as credit risk, can play a decisive role in the overall assessment of a bank’s viability. These findings underpin the critical role of judgement in adapting supervisory frameworks to evolving risks and systemic conditions, providing flexibility at both the individual and system-wide levels.

title: Strength Characteristics and Microstructural Features of Unsaturated Expansive Soil over a Wide Suction Range
affiliations: North China University of Water Resources and Electric Power, North China University of Water Resources and Electric Power, North China University of Water Resources and Electric Power, North China University of Water Resources and Electric Power, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Shandong University of Science and Technology

detail.title: Strength Characteristics and Microstructural Features of Unsaturated Expansive Soil over a Wide Suction Range
detail.abstract: To reveal the macro–micro mechanical response mechanism of unsaturated expansive soil over a wide suction range, soil samples were collected from the embankment of the Dengzhou section of the South-to-North Water Diversion Middle Route Project in China. GDS triaxial shear tests were conducted under suction levels ranging from 0 to 38,000 kPa, together with mercury intrusion porosimetry (MIP) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM), to investigate the microstructural evolution of the soil. Random forest (RF) and artificial neural network (ANN) models were introduced to establish cross-scale quantitative relationships between macroscopic mechanical parameters and microstructural indices.The results indicate that the failure strength, especially cohesion, and shear strength increase gradually with suction. MIP results show that the pore structure becomes denser with increasing suction, and the microscopic void ratio under high suction increases by up to 35% compared with that under low suction. The relationships between suction and void ratio, as well as those between void ratio and shear strength parameters, can be well described by exponential functions, revealing a synergistic evolution path from increased suction to decreased void ratio and enhanced strength parameters. Both RF and ANN models effectively predict the shear strength parameters, while the ANN model exhibits better fitting performance, error control, and stability in the suction range of 3,290–38,000 kPa, indicating its superior applicability under high-suction conditions.This study clarifies the intrinsic coupling relationship between macroscopic mechanical behavior and microstructural evolution of unsaturated expansive soil, providing theoretical support and new insights for refined prediction and engineering application under varying suction conditions.

title: Immigrant Business Owner Activity in the Pandemic and Recovery
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA)

detail.title: Immigrant Business Owner Activity in the Pandemic and Recovery
detail.abstract: The paper provides a descriptive analysis of both the early impacts of COVID on business activity among immigrants and the economic recovery over the next few years. The findings indicate that immigrant business owners were disproportionately affected by COVID in the first month of the pandemic when mandated shutdowns through social distancing restrictions were the most severe. Immigrant business activity recovered somewhat inconsistently through the end of 2020 but started a longer-term upward trend in both absolute terms and relative terms over the next few years. By the end of 2024, the number of active immigrant business owners increased to 3.9 million compared with 3.0 million just prior to the start of the pandemic. Growth in the Construction, Transportation, Professional and Business Services, and Financial Activities industry groups fueled total growth in immigrant business activity during the recovery period. The percentage of the labor force owning an active business is 3.5 percentage points higher than U.S. born active business ownership rates, which is larger than the 1.8 percentage point gap before the pandemic started.

title: Airline Merger Effects Along the Exposure Distribution

detail.title: Airline Merger Effects Along the Exposure Distribution
detail.abstract: I evaluate the competitive effects of four major U.S. airline mergers (2008-2013) using a continuous difference-in-differences model. Standard merger retrospectives typically rely on binary treatment classifications that collapse important variation in competitive exposure. I construct three continuous route-level exposure measures — simulated ∆HHI (direct competitive overlap), merger share (the merging carriers' combined presence), and non-overlap merger share (merger share on routes where only one merging carrier operated) — and estimate dose-response curves for each. Results reveal substantial heterogeneity both across mergers and within each merger across the exposure distribution, with the three measures yielding different conclusions, as each captures a distinct competitive channel.

title: The Causal Effects of Federal Work-Study Offers on College Enrollment and Program Participation
affiliations: Columbia University, Columbia University and American University

detail.title: The Causal Effects of Federal Work-Study Offers on College Enrollment and Program Participation
detail.abstract: Federal Work-Study (FWS) is a distinctive type of financial aid, intended to both reduce financial constraints and improve access to career-relevant job opportunities. Prior research on FWS has primarily focused on post-enrollment, post-program-participation outcomes, leaving potential upstream margins of impact unexplored. Using a unique administrative data source tracking FWS offers, enrollment, and participation from the date of financial aid application, we study the causal impacts of receiving an FWS offer at a large public college system including both two- and four-year campuses. We use a difference-in-differences approach comparing FWS-eligible aid applicants to similar ineligible applicants, who apply before and after an arbitrary date after which FWS availability is limited. Though we find no effects of FWS offers on enrollment for the full sample, we do find significant increases in enrollment for community college students and independent students. We also find that receiving an FWS offer before the academic year begins increases the likelihood of subsequently holding an FWS job by 27 percentage points– a large effect, but far from complete take-up. The offer-induced increase in FWS job holding is also heterogenous across subgroups. Our results provide new insights on which student populations may be most sensitive to an FWS offer, and demonstrate that enrollment impacts can occur even in the context of overall low program take-up.

title: A Cross-National Test of Productive Configuration as the Primary Determinant of Democratic Regime Type

detail.title: A Cross-National Test of Productive Configuration as the Primary Determinant of Democratic Regime Type

declarations.ethicsApproval: The research was conducted using publicly accessible information found online. No interviews were conducted.
declarations.funderStatement: The research was funded exclusively by the author.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a cross-national test of the infrastructure-determines hypothesis: that the productive configuration of a society-specifically, the relative dominance of its four infrastructure layers (Extractive, Manufacturing, Networked, and FIRE)-is the primary determinant of democratic regime type. Using V-Dem Liberal Democracy Index data for 179 countries (1975-2022), World Bank national accounts, and Quality of Government project data, I test this hypothesis against four leading alternative explanations: modernization theory (income), ethnic fractionalization theory, resource curse theory, and civilizational identity. The infrastructure-regime bivariate correlation is r = .612 (N = 179), outperforming per-capita income (r = .481), ethnic fractionalization (r =-.183), resource rents (r =-.224), and civilizational classification (η = .31). After controlling for infrastructure configuration, ethnic fractionalization drops to a partial r of .008 (p = .814), statistically indistinguishable from zero. One-way ANOVA with infrastructure layer dominance as the grouping variable accounts for 45.2 percent of crossnational variance in democratic regime type (η² = .452, p < .001). A path analysis estimates that infrastructure exercises its effect 53 percent through the ideology-mediated pathway and 47 percent through direct institutional demand (Sobel z = 3.20, p = .001). These findings are robust to fixed-effects panel estimation (β = .009, lag 5, p < .001) and to instrumental variables estimation using latitude as an instrument for infrastructure configuration (first-stage F = 19.88). The implications for the study of democratic backsliding are discussed.

reference: Forthcoming in Friso Bostoen (ed.), Global Platform Regulation (Cambridge University Press)
title: India's Evolving Approach to Platform Regulation
affiliations: European University Institute - Department of Law (LAW) and Jindal Global Law School

detail.title: India's Evolving Approach to Platform Regulation

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming in Friso Bostoen (ed.), Global Platform Regulation (Cambridge University Press)

detail.abstract: India's digital markets are unique due to the simultaneous presence of a vibrant domestic start-up ecosystem, a significant informal sector comprising small businesses who are users of digital platforms, and large conglomerates. Regulations in India have sought to balance the interests of consumers and business users while ensuring that the country remains an attractive destination for investments from big tech. Hence, attempts at regulating platforms have been cautious, as reflected by the withdrawal of the proposed ex ante Digital Competition Bill in 2025. However, ex post competition enforcement has been strengthened through amendments to the Indian Competition Act in 2023, even though enforcement remains slow. A different approach adopted in India is the creation of Digital Public Infrastructures to ensure participation of more players. This chapter discusses these developments in platform regulation and regulatory authorities' balancing of different goals, given the characteristics of digital markets in India.

title: Nine Lives vs. Man's Best Friend: What's a Cat's Value of a Statistical Life (VSL) Compared to a Dog's?
affiliations: and Brock University

detail.title: Nine Lives vs. Man's Best Friend: What's a Cat's Value of a Statistical Life (VSL) Compared to a Dog's?

declarations.ethicsApproval: Brock University Research Ethics Board (REB): #24-322.
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: Cats and dogs are the most common household pets in the United States (and, by most measures, globally), with many owners claiming their pets as close companions, if not additional family members. Spending on pets (including food, toys, and veterinary services) is big business, with 2025 estimates in the US alone as high as $157 billion. Yet for all their importance in the economy and in many peoples' daily lives, there is very little empirical research investigating a shadow price for the statistical value of a cat life (VSCL), or the statistical value of a dog life (VSDL). The primary objective of this study is to determine empirical valuations for both of these measures, through traditional contingent valuation survey techniques. Uniquely, we do this by querying both cat and dog owners at the same time, and in the same survey, so that a secondary objective of this research is to finally answer the perennial question of which pet is valued more highly by the American public: cats or dogs.

reference: Center for Governance and Markets Paper No. DA2-2026
title: Reimagining US Foreign Aid: From Short-Term Relief to Lasting Change
affiliations: University of Pittsburgh

detail.title: Reimagining US Foreign Aid: From Short-Term Relief to Lasting Change

publicationDetails.detailsText: Center for Governance and Markets Paper No. DA2-2026
publicationDetails.journalName: Center for Governance & Markets Paper Series

detail.abstract: Over two decades’ worth of US foreign assistance in the Middle East has produced mixed results. The United States has spent tens of billions of dollars on rebuilding infrastructure, strengthening governance, and promoting stability in countries such as Iraq and Afghanistan. Yet much of this investment has failed to create long-term development. Schools were constructed without trained teachers, power plants were operated without maintenance capacity, and bureaucratic inefficiency consumed vast portions of aid budgets. This pattern reflects a deeper flaw in the global aid system. Large, top-down programs often prioritize donor visibility and bureaucratic compliance over local ownership and measurable outcomes. As a result, aid has too often fostered dependency rather than dignity, and inefficiency rather than innovation. A reimagined aid strategy must focus on empowering local actors, rewarding outcomes instead of inputs, and linking development directly to human agency and self-determination. By embracing smaller, faster, and more accountable funding mechanisms, the United States can align its aid strategy with both its values and its strategic interest.

title: Paid Annual Leave and the Incidence of Part-Time Employment
affiliations: University of Granada, University of Girona - Department of Economics and University of Girona

detail.title: Paid Annual Leave and the Incidence of Part-Time Employment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no conflict of interest.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how statutory paid annual leave affects aggregate employment and the composition of work across part-time and full-time jobs. We develop a search-and-matching model with two job types in which paid leave generates disruption costs for firms that are larger in full-time positions, while also providing utility to workers. The model predicts that paid leave increases the relative attractiveness of part-time jobs and shifts employment toward shorter-hour contracts, while leaving the response of aggregate employment ambiguous. Using a crosscountry panel from the World Bank covering 2005-2019, we find robust evidence that more generous paid leave is associated with a higher share of part-time employment. In contrast, the relationship with aggregate employment is weak: while bivariate correlations are negative, the effect becomes small and statistically insignificant once country and time fixed effects are included. Overall, paid leave primarily affects employment composition rather than aggregate employment levels.

title: The Working Life of a Teacher: Lessons from the Danish Matched Student-Teacher Data
affiliations: Aarhus University, Aarhus University - Department of Economics and Business Economics and Aarhus University - Department of Economics and Business Economics

detail.title: The Working Life of a Teacher: Lessons from the Danish Matched Student-Teacher Data
detail.abstract: This paper uses Danish register-based matched student–teacher data to characterize public school teachers and their working conditions. We document gender segregation across subjects and grades, with female teachers dominating Danish instruction and male teachers more common in upper grade math. Teachers select into subjects based on subject specific academic skills, yet a notable share has weak prerequisite skills. Teachers often specialize in student age groups but teach multiple subjects. Those with stronger skills tend to work in schools with similarly skilled colleagues. These findings provide new insights relevant for interpreting education research and designing policies to improve teacher retention and wellbeing.

title: Path Dependency in Interest Group Representation? A Historical Institutionalist approach to the European Social Dialogue

detail.title: Path Dependency in Interest Group Representation? A Historical Institutionalist approach to the European Social Dialogue
detail.abstract: This paper applies a Historical Institutionalist approach to the European Union’s supranational social policy, focusing on the Social Dialogue framework. It argues that Historical Institutionalism better explains dynamics of change and stability than neo-functionalism or intergovernmentalism, which tend to overlook new institutional arrangement in the informal spheres of policy making and implementation, amounting to institutional innovations. The study traces the evolution of the Social Dialogue from its consensual beginnings in the mid-1980s, through institutionalization under the Maastricht Treaty, to the present, where consultation has largely replaced substantive participation. Despite limited legislative impact, social partners continue engagement, primarily as a channel for lobbying and representation. Using Historical Institutionalist concepts of gaps and increasing returns, the paper examines path dependency in the Social Dialogue, testing whether long-term development has produced persistent gaps and whether the limited legislative progress constrains substantial reform of the regulatory framework.

title: Capital Holdup, Job Creation, and Skill Supply under Search Frictions
affiliations: and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Capital Holdup, Job Creation, and Skill Supply under Search Frictions

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: There has been renewed interest in revitalizing manufacturing, yet policy often confronts a circular challenge: firms hesitate to expand because they cannot reliably find suitably skilled workers (e.g., STEM-trained), while workers are reluctant to acquire those skills when jobs remain limited. This raises a policy question: intervene at the firm margin or the worker margin, or both? We study this question by extending Acemoglu and Shimer (1999) to a two-sector open-economy. The key friction is capital holdup: firms invest upfront to create jobs, but sunk investment weakens their wage bargaining positions, discouraging investment ex-ante. Because manufacturing is more capital intensive, holdup is more severe, leaving manufacturing employment inefficiently low. In the calibrated model, this inefficiency-induced industrial employment shortfall is about 1 percent of total employment – roughly one-fifth of LAC-East Asia gap. When Hosios condition holds, the optimal policy can be solely on the firm side: an investment subsidy financed by an employment tax on firms. When Hosios condition fails, an additional wedge distorting workers’ sectoral choices emerges, and targeted training subsidies become welfare-improving.

title: The Compliance Chasm: How Global Traceability Systems Extract Value from African Producers - and How Sovereign Data Logic Solution can Fix it

detail.title: The Compliance Chasm: How Global Traceability Systems Extract Value from African Producers - and How Sovereign Data Logic Solution can Fix it
detail.abstract:
Although traceability is becoming a crucial component of global trade, its economic benefits are still not equally distributed. This study highlights a "Compliance Chasm" in which data generation expenses are borne by African producers while value is obtained later on by external actors. The paper presents Sovereign Data Logics as a principles guaranteeing that originating economies own and profit from their trade data as a solution to this asymmetry. It suggests a modular, non-coding data governance structure that connects high-stakes global standards with low-tech production realities. 

The paper uses the Kaduna-Lagos grain corridor as a case study to show how switching from compliance-driven to sovereignty-driven architectures might unleash "Traceability Dividends." The study comes to the conclusion that transforming traceability from an extraction tool into a platform for active data governance and national value retention is vital for the future of trade in the Global South. This research establishes a foundational theoretical basis for applied system architectures, including TerraVerify, designed to bridge the data-trust gap in global extractives. Disclosure: This research employ Generative AI for manuscript optimization and iterative design refinement. The core methodology (DSR), the "Compliance Chasm" theory, and all empirical case study analysis remain the author's original work.

title: Amplifying Long-Horizon Equity Returns: Evidence from Long-Term Equity Anticipation Securities (LEAPS)
affiliations: University of Connecticut- Finance Department

detail.title: Amplifying Long-Horizon Equity Returns: Evidence from Long-Term Equity Anticipation Securities (LEAPS)
detail.abstract: Examining the return dynamics of long-dated at-the-money call options (LEAPS) on the SPY ETF across 30 years of rolling two-year windows under a quadratic regression framework, we document statistically and economically significant convexity in realized call returns that is robust to heteroskedasticity correction, outlier trimming, and non-overlapping window estimation. A modest 5% core-satellite allocation to LEAPS adds approximately 432 basis points to mean two-year index portfolio returns. Convexity is economically meaningful only over multiyear holding horizons, not in one-year allocations and short-put-overlay strategies. These findings support our claim that LEAPS calls harness persistent convex positive drifts in realized long-horizon aggregate equity market returns due to productivity growth and policy stability, unlike the noisy and transient short horizon returns.

title: Do Job Postings Show Early Labor‑Market Effects of AI?
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York

detail.title: Do Job Postings Show Early Labor‑Market Effects of AI?

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
As generative AI tools become more widely used, a key issue is the technology’s impact on labor demand. Where might we find evidence of that impact? In this post, we examine whether early evidence of AI’s effect on the labor market appears in firms’ job postings. We combine an occupational measure of AI exposure with detailed U.S. job-posting data from Lightcast, which aggregates listings from company career pages, national and local job boards, and job-listing aggregators. Using this data, we test whether postings for AI-exposed occupations declined disproportionately since the release of ChatGPT in late 2022. We find that, while overall hiring has slowed since then, the evidence from job postings provides little indication of a distinct AI-driven decline in labor demand.

To view post: https://libertystreeteconomics.newyorkfed.org/2026/05/do-job-postings-show-early-labor-market-effects-of-ai/

reference: GMU Working Paper in Economics (forthcoming); Kansas Journal of Law & Public Policy, Vol. 8, pp. 1–21 (1998)
title: Economic Analysis of Labor Markets: A Framework for Analyzing Employment Law Issues
affiliations: George Mason University - Antonin Scalia Law School and University of Kansas - School of Business

detail.title: Economic Analysis of Labor Markets: A Framework for Analyzing Employment Law Issues

publicationDetails.journalName: George Mason University Department of Economics Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: Kansas Journal of Law & Public Policy, Vol. 8, pp. 1–21 (1998)

detail.abstract:
Employment law has emerged as a major area of litigation in both the federal and state courts. In an effort to help judges understand many of the policy issues underlying the current surge in litigation, the Law and Organizational Economics Center of the University of Kansas sponsored a conference on “The Economic Analysis of State Employment Law Issues.” The goal of the conference was to present judges with a variety of viewpoints on major areas of employment law, including the employment contract, discrimination and sexual harassment, and workplace safety. Nationally recognized scholars in those areas were recruited to present their views. In order to appreciate the policy analysis of those fairly specialized issues, it is necessary to first provide a foundation in the economics of the labor markets. 

Our discussion is organized as follows. Section II is a brief overview of the determination of market wages through the interaction of labor market supply and demand, with an application to the impact of minimum wage legislation. Section III considers the fundamental question of whether labor markets really work the way the theory predicts — in the sense of recognizing and pricing the terms and conditions of employment contracts. Particular attention is paid to the market incentives for employers to provide a safe workplace and to not fire employees at random. Section IV reviews the economics of employment discrimination. Section V offers some concluding comments about the role of economic analysis in judicial decision making.

title: Governing The Black Box: AI Liability Allocation in Data Center and Cloud Infrastructure Contracts
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Governing The Black Box: AI Liability Allocation in Data Center and Cloud Infrastructure Contracts
detail.abstract:
The proliferation of autonomous AI systems within data center operations, such as governing cooling optimisation, capacity planning, and real-time SLA monitoring, has outpaced the contractual frameworks designed to allocate risk when those systems fail. As the Asia-Pacific data center market expands toward 57 GW of capacity by 2030, driven by hyperscale cloud deployment and AI inference workloads, the question of who bears liability when an autonomous system causes infrastructure downtime, data loss, or SLA breach has become commercially urgent and legally unanswered. 

This paper makes three contributions. First, it maps the deployment of autonomous AI systems across three core data center functions, such as thermal management, predictive capacity planning, and incident response automation, and identifies the liability trigger points embedded in each. Second, it analyses the standard publicly available terms of the three dominant hyperscale cloud providers (AWS, Azure, and GCP) against the negotiated contract landscape documented by Hon, Millard, and Walden, demonstrating that standard terms are structurally silent on AI-caused failures: liability caps, warranty disclaimers, and SLA credit mechanisms were not designed for autonomous systems and do not adequately allocate AIspecific risk. Third, it conducts a comparative jurisdictional gap analysis across Malaysia and Singapore, showing that neither jurisdiction has developed binding legal instruments capable of resolving AI liability in commercial infrastructure contracts.

Drawing on systems theory approaches to AI value chain responsibility, joint controllership analysis in AI-as-a-Service contexts, and shared liability frameworks for complex technologies, this paper proposes a model clause framework of three contractual instruments tailored for APAC data center agreements: an AI System Disclosure and Classification Schedule; a tiered liability structure with AI-specific carve-outs from the standard fee cap; and an AI Incident Audit and Root Cause Analysis obligation. The paper argues that the governance gap is not merely technical but structural: AI systems in data centers generate efficiency gains captured entirely by providers while catastrophic failure costs are absorbed by customers under terms that predate the autonomous systems now operating within them.

reference: Temple University Legal Studies Research Paper Rutgers Law Review (forthcoming)
title: The End Of Citizenship As We Have Known It
affiliations: Temple University - James E. Beasley School of Law

detail.title: The End Of Citizenship As We Have Known It

publicationDetails.detailsText: Temple University Legal Studies Research Paper Rutgers Law Review (forthcoming)
publicationDetails.journalName: Temple University Beasley School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Working from Linda Bosniak's canonical framing of citizenship, this essay rebalances the four perspectives of legal status, rights, political activity, and collective identity in light of recent developments. The essay argues that citizenship as rights, political activity, and collective identity is now in a state of freefall. While these three elements are dissipating, the salience of citizenship as legal status has magnified. This is not a normatively neutral adjustment. Rights, political activity, and collective identity have supplied a virtuous tripod for the institution. It was only on this tripod that citizenship’s valence as legal status has been morally sustainable. It is the legal status of citizenship that centers citizenship’s formalism, which has no essential normative content. Status also highlights the binary nature of citizenship status. Some people have it, some people do not. So long as privileges attach to the status, citizenship translates into inequality. That inequality has been tolerable so long as its virtuous functions remained in place. Once they are gone, citizenship loses its normativity.

The essay then turns to the development of citizenship alternatives. As citizenship on the domestic front faced new challenges, some sketched the possibility of transnational substitutes as a byproduct of globalization. Although transnational and non-state venues may present citizenship-type attributes over the longer run, any such shift will be tectonic. Transnational developments have been a stressor on citizenship within the state, disrupting the dimensions of rights, politics, and identity. But those global spheres have not developed to carry the weight of an institution that was itself centuries in the making. In the meantime, we are left with a kind of citizenship interregnum, a scary prospect against the scary challenges that the world faces now on so many fronts.

title: Why is Deferred Acceptance (Almost) Always Implemented in Non-Manipulable School Choice?
affiliations: University of Montreal

detail.title: Why is Deferred Acceptance (Almost) Always Implemented in Non-Manipulable School Choice?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author (Lars Ehlers) declares that he has no relevant or material financial interests that relate to the research described in this paper.

detail.abstract: A school choice problem consists of a set of students with their preferences and a set of schools with their fixed capacities and priorities. The trade-off between efficiency and stability has been widely discussed-the student-proposing deferred-acceptance algorithm satisfies stability but violates efficiency while the top-trading-cycles algorithm satisfies efficiency but violates stability. It is natural to require that when there is no trade-off between efficiency and stability, then an assignment satisfying both properties shall be chosen-which we call efficiency-and-stability. We show that for non-manipulable school choice mechanisms this unambiguously favors the student-proposing deferredacceptance (DA-)mechanism. On the one hand, there exists no other mechanism which is efficient, non-manipulable and complies with efficiency-and-stability. On the other hand, we show that the student-proposing deferred-acceptance mechanism is the only (efficient-and-stable and) non-manipulable mechanism excluding blocking pairs with unassigned students. This helps to explain the puzzle why in practice centralized clearing houses have implemented the DA-mechanism while being reluctant in adopting efficient mechanisms other than the DA-mechanism.

reference: TIAA Institute Research Paper Series No 234
title: The Impact of Spousal Social Security Claiming Decisions on the Financial Shock of Widowhood
affiliations: George Mason University - School of Policy, Government, and International Affairs

detail.title: The Impact of Spousal Social Security Claiming Decisions on the Financial Shock of Widowhood

publicationDetails.detailsText: TIAA Institute Research Paper Series No 234

detail.abstract: This paper presents evidence suggesting that delayed Social Security claiming by husbands-resulting in an actuarially enhanced benefitattenuates the financial shock of widowhood for their wives. Under Social Security survivor benefit rules, primary earners (usually husbands) pass on the actuarial adjustments from delayed claiming to their surviving spouses. Using a staggered difference-indifferences approach, I find women whose husbands delayed claiming to full retirement age or later face a post-widowhood increase of 6.9 percentage points in the probability of falling below the 5th percentile of the pre-widowhood income distribution. This effect is almost 12 percent smaller for each year of delayed claiming by the husband (though the attenuation is concentrated in the first 4 years of widowhood). The general findings are robust to instrumenting for the husband's claiming age using the loosening of the retirement earnings test in 2000-a policy change that incentivized earlier claiming.

title: Subsidy Bundles
affiliations: University of Illinois at Chicago - Department of Economics

detail.title: Subsidy Bundles
detail.abstract: A common problem with subsidizing socially beneficial goods is that many subsidies flow to inframarginal agents. In this paper, I describe how the problem of subsidizing multiple goods (or actions) is similar to the problem facing a multi-product monopolist. Bundling can allow multiproduct monopolists to capture consumer surplus above the optimal individual-good prices, especially when the demand for products is negatively correlated across individuals. Applying a similar argument to the government's problem, I characterize conditions under which pure or mixed bundles of subsidies can improve the cost-effectiveness of incentive programs. To conclude, I use simulations to compare the performance of bundled versus unbundled subsidies in two settings: (i) green durable good adoption in the United States, and (ii) a conditional cash transfer program in Indonesia.

title: Exposure-Aware Governance: Adaptive Administrative Cadence and Participation Stability in Multi-Program Public Benefits Systems

detail.title: Exposure-Aware Governance: Adaptive Administrative Cadence and Participation Stability in Multi-Program Public Benefits Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study used publicly available aggregate administrative and policy data and did not involve human subjects research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Public benefit programs impose repeated procedural requirements—verification cycles, recertification deadlines, documentation requests—that generate cumulative administrative burden over time. Existing governance frameworks evaluate these requirements episodically, at discrete eligibility determinations, rather than as dynamic processes whose stability depends on the relationship between administrative load and recovery capacity. This paper develops a formal model of administrative exposure and derives adaptive cadence adjustment as a participation-stabilizing governance policy. A cross-system amplification result establishes that multi-program participation increases steady-state administrative exposure even when each program’s individual requirements are reasonable—a structural consequence of uncoordinated procedural cadence. Adaptive governance produces lower expected exposure and lower procedural exit probability than fixed-cadence regimes, while expanding the set of conditions under which participation remains administratively viable, particularly for multi-program enrollees near the collapse threshold. The framework is grounded empirically in the Medicaid unwinding period (2023–2024). Across states, ex parte renewal rates—the share of eligibility determinations completed without participant-facing documentation requirements—were inversely associated with procedural disenrollment rates, consistent with the recovery-capacity mechanism the model formalizes. Complementary computational experiments further suggest that upper-tail exposure concentration may emerge as a leading indicator of administrative instability before aggregate burden metrics visibly deteriorate. The central implication is that governance quality in benefit administration should be evaluated not only on eligibility accuracy, but on whether administrative design sustains eligible participation over time.

title: Born into Doubt: Why Ghana Should Reject Mandatory Paternity Testing

detail.title: Born into Doubt: Why Ghana Should Reject Mandatory Paternity Testing

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The are no known conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study did not require ethical approval as it did not include human or animal subjects and relied entirely on already published secondary information.
declarations.funderStatement: The work did not receive external funding. The author self-funded the work.

detail.abstract: A proposal has been advanced in Ghanaian public discourse for the introduction of mandatory paternity DNA testing for every child born in a healthcare facility, accompanied by the criminalisation of paternity fraud. No bill has yet been laid before Parliament. This commentary engages with the proposal as it has been publicly articulated and argues that it is unnecessary, constitutionally incoherent, discriminatory, and harmful to the welfare of the child. Ghanaian law already provides a calibrated framework for the resolution of paternity disputes under the Evidence Act 1975, the Children's Act 1998, and the Courts Act 1993, in which DNA testing is available through judicial order with the welfare of the child at the centre. The proposal would displace this framework with a regime of administrative coercion at the hospital door, replacing a rebuttable presumption of paternity with a precondition for the legal recognition of the newborn. It would breach the equality guarantees of Article 17 of the 1992 Constitution and Article 18(3) of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights by interrogating paternity while treating maternity as unquestionable, codifying a presumption of female deceit. It would collapse the distinction between honest mistake, biological anomaly, and deliberate fraud, abandoning the principle of mens rea. It would interfere with the bodily integrity of mothers and infants in conditions that preclude free and informed consent. As a Private Member's Bill, it would fail the test of Article 108. The empirical foundation advanced in its support is a misreading of the scientific literature on paternity discrepancies. The paper concludes by setting out a constructive alternative grounded in public education and civil remedies for proven deception. Ghana should reject the proposal of mandatory paternity DNA testing.

title: Optimizing Retirement Financial Strategies: Integrating Annuities, Defined Contribution Plans, and Long-Term Care Costs
