declarations.clinicalTrialRegistration: Not applicable. This manuscript is a policy and methodological analysis of the statutory structure of the Rural Health Transformation Program (Public Law 119-21, Section 71401) and the measurement requirements implied by its cooperative agreement reporting framework. It does not describe a clinical trial, intervention study, or any prospective study of human subjects. No clinical trial registration is required or available.

detail.abstract: The Rural Health Transformation Program, authorized under Section 71401 of Public Law 119-21 and administered by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) as a cooperative agreement, distributes $50 billion to state recipients over fiscal years 2026 through 2030. The authorizing statute and the CMS Notice of Funding Opportunity impose three categorical ceilings on each state's allocation: direct patient care payments cannot exceed 15 percent, infrastructure investments cannot exceed 20 percent, and state administrative expenses cannot exceed 10 percent. We show that these ceilings yield a structural lower bound: at least 65 percent of every state allocationapproximately $32.5 billion in aggregate over the program horizon-must flow into use categories that cannot be evaluated by counting facilities built or services paid for. The 65 percent bucket comprises workforce development, technology-enabled care delivery, evidence-based prevention, behavioral health, and innovative care models. Each of these categories requires facilitylevel outcome measurement against an external ground truth to be evaluable under cooperative agreement reporting requirements. We formalize the resulting measurement function, examine first-year state plan data for evidence of the predicted spending pattern, address five plausible counterarguments, and identify the structural component-a translation layer mapping CMS Healthcare Cost Report Information System (HCRIS) data to per-facility benchmark claims-whose construction is necessary for the program to demonstrate effectiveness. The Critical Access Hospital subsegment is identified as the architecturally tractable testbed by virtue of its regulatory uniformity under 42 CFR § 485.

title: When Manufacturing Cannot Return: A Threshold Theorem for Trade-Induced Deindustrialization
affiliations: University of Brasília (UnB) and Instituto Brasileiro de Ensino, Desenvolvimento e Pesquisa (IDP)

detail.title: When Manufacturing Cannot Return: A Threshold Theorem for Trade-Induced Deindustrialization

declarations.funderStatement: João Gabriel thanks to the financial support from CNPQ (Grant n. 155571/2025-7).

detail.abstract: An intermediate-income economy facing competition from a dominant manufacturing core can lose manufacturing as a long-run attractor at a sharp threshold in the core’s share of world manufacturing. We characterise this threshold s¯ in a three-region Dixit–Stiglitz economy with iceberg trade costs and a frequency-dependent agglomeration externality γxM(1 − xM), and show that it is determined by the saddle-node condition pM(s¯)+γ/4 = c¯B(wB)+πA, in which the maximum agglomeration bonus exactly offsets the gap between the world manufacturing price and the intermediate economy’s minimum average cost plus the agricultural return. The same threshold arises from four different mathematical lenses—a saddle-node bifurcation, a loss of Markov-chain irreducibility, a primal–dual stability boundary, and a fixation-probability collapse—each making visible a distinct consequence of crossing s¯. Above s¯, agricultural specialisation is the unique globally stable steady state. Irreversibility is established deterministically through exponential convergence of the replicator orbit with explicit rate λ = |pM(sC) − c¯B(wB) − πA|; stochastically through almost-sure absorption of the diffusion approximation at the agricultural boundary, identified as an exit boundary in Feller’s sense; and ergodically through Cesàro convergence of the empirical sectoral distribution. A weighted trade hypergraph identifies the world-price vertex as the unique minimum transversal of the policy system, and an abstract max-flow / min-cut argument bounds the policy gain achievable under any binding budget by the world-price capacity. Sector-specific subsidies cannot reverse lock-in above s¯; policies that act on the threshold itself—reducing manufacturing average cost or strengthening agglomeration—can shift it.

title: Money, Markets, and the Barrel: Evaluating the Predictive Content of Divisia M4 for U.S. Crude-Oil Price Growth
affiliations: University of Northern Iowa

detail.title: Money, Markets, and the Barrel: Evaluating the Predictive Content of Divisia M4 for U.S. Crude-Oil Price Growth
detail.abstract: The recent volatility of U.S. oil prices has raised interest in what actually drives these short-term price changes. This study examines whether money growth helps explain or predict oil price movements, after accounting for major economic factors. The study uses monthly data from 2003 to 2025, with variables including the dollar value, market volatility, supply chain pressure, interest rates, and oil production. A simple regression approach was used to find which variables had the largest impact. The dollar index and headline inflation had the strongest impact on oil prices, and money growth was not a significant factor, but lagging money growth data did shave some forecasting value. Given the complexity of oil markets and their many influences, additional research is encouraged to assess how these relationships hold up under different economic conditions.

title: Adaptive Causal Inference for Higher-Order Difference-in-Differences Designs

detail.title: Adaptive Causal Inference for Higher-Order Difference-in-Differences Designs
detail.abstract: This paper develops a partition selection framework for choosing among differencein-differences (DiD), triple differences (DDD), and higher-order designs. The framework formalizes when additional categorical dimensions should enter the benchmark comparison structure, rather than being left to residual heterogeneity analysis. An identification-aware information criterion selects the comparison partition by combining post-treatment cross-validated fit, pre-treatment placebo discrepancy, a complexity penalty, and a support rule. In a benchmark design with common timing and categorical covariates, the selected partition is consistent for the minimal valid comparison structure, and the resulting subgroup ATT estimator is asymptotically equivalent to the oracle estimator. Extensions cover doubly robust estimation, staggered adoption, and constrained tree refinements. Monte Carlo simulations show that the criterion reliably selects the valid comparison structure and improves finite-sample performance. Empirical applications demonstrate how the method provides transparent, data-driven benchmarks for applied DiD and DDD practice.

title: Coordination vs. Competition: Local Government Centralization and Metropolitan Growth

detail.title: Coordination vs. Competition: Local Government Centralization and Metropolitan Growth
detail.abstract: This paper estimates the causal effect of local government centralization on metropolitan growth in the United States. I measure centralization at the metropolitan statistical area level using an index constructed from local government employment shares, combining the number of governments, largest-government share, Herfindahl concentration, and entropy. To address endogenous local government organization, I instrument centralization with post office closures induced by the Postal Service’s introduction of Rural Free Delivery in 1902. The instrument predicts persistent modern decentralization, consistent with historical settlement dispersion shaping annexation and incorporation margins. I find that centralization increases population and employment growth, raises local government employment, and increases total and tax revenue. Centralized MSAs are also less likely to host data centers. The results favor a coordination-failure interpretation of local government fragmentation over a Tiebout-style competition mechanism or a simple economies-of-scale channel.

title: Cloud Seeding and Hailstorm Damage: A Dynamic Panel Analysis of Alberta's Hail Suppression Program, 2011-2020
affiliations: and Western University

detail.title: Cloud Seeding and Hailstorm Damage: A Dynamic Panel Analysis of Alberta's Hail Suppression Program, 2011-2020
detail.abstract: We estimate the effect of cloud seeding on hailstorm intensity using radartracked observations of 175 storms over Alberta's Hail Suppression Program region between 2011 and 2020. A dynamic system-GMM panel specification with three lags of log vertically integrated liquid (VIL), individual storm fixed effects, and a 32-minute physical lag on the seeding indicator yields an average within-storm reduction in log VIL of 3 to 5 per cent, robust to alternative lag choices and to a placebo test that fails to replicate the result in 99 per cent of randomized treatment assignments. Allowing the seeding effect to vary across within-storm quartiles of proximity to peak VIL reveals strong heterogeneity: the effect is-11 to-16 per cent in the early-storm quartile, near zero at mid-storm, and +6 per cent at the storm's peak intensity. Translating this pattern into Calgary's annual hail losses through the benefitcost framework of Porter (2023), and applying explicit incomplete-coverage

title: The Role of Budget Support in Growth and Adjustment

detail.title: The Role of Budget Support in Growth and Adjustment

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The use of IMF credit for budgetary financing (budget support) has surged in Extended Credit Facility (ECF) arrangements with low-income countries (LICs) post pandemic, yet its role in growth and adjustment remains understudied. This paper provides the first systematic analysis of budget support across all 100 ECFs approved since the PRGT’s inception in 2010. We develop a reduced-form model that captures how budget support affects the growth-reserves trade-off, where budget support substitutes for domestic financing and thus reduces crowding-out in domestic credit markets. The simulations are performed under wide parameter uncertainty reflecting limited evidence for LICs. Staggered difference-in-differences estimates on completed programs validate the model’s predictions, revealing average treatment effects on growth of 3.4 percentage points but 1.3 months of imports slower reserve accumulation by program end. These results fall at the upper bound of simulations, consistent with severe financing constraints in treated LICs. Budget support shows weak positive effects on fiscal and external adjustments, though not statistically robust, suggesting that it does not weaken consolidation incentives and that sustainable adjustment depends primarily on policy strength and fundamentals rather than financing modalities. Critically, budget support acts as a catalyst contingent on program completion: off-track programs experience particularly adverse growth outcomes. Findings underscore the need for careful consideration of growth-adjustment trade-offs in program design. Short-term growth support must be balanced against building external buffers with country-specific circumstances determining appropriate financing modalities.

title: The Macro-Fiscal Impacts of Post-Disaster IMF Financing
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: The Macro-Fiscal Impacts of Post-Disaster IMF Financing

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The IMF provides macro-stabilizing liquidity when others cannot. The IMF has developed a set of instruments designed to provide rapid financial assistance to countries facing urgent balance of payments needs without requiring a full-fledged economic program, triggered by exogenous natural disasters shocks. We evaluate the impact of IMF emergency financing after natural disaster using a synthetic control method. The results show that IMF post-disaster financing supports a faster GDP recovery, with an implied average IMF post-disaster multiplier larger than 1. The findings suggest strong liquidity and catalytic effects, enabling countercyclical fiscal responses. However, the resulting increase in public debt underscores the need for credible medium-term fiscal plans and post-disaster consolidation to maintain debt sustainability.

title: Fiscal Decentralization and Cyclicality in Latin America
affiliations: , Bank of Canada, Financial Stability Department, Financial Studies Division,  and

detail.title: Fiscal Decentralization and Cyclicality in Latin America

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Using a newly constructed database of highly granular regional-level budgets, this paper documents the growing relevance of regional governments in Latin America over the past three decades and evaluates the implications for fiscal cyclicality. We find that regional governments exhibit lower revenue elasticity to national GDP than central governments, primarily due to the limited cyclicality of transfers. On the expenditure side, while overall elasticity is comparable to central governments, fiscal adjustment occurs through capital expenditures. We also show that transfers appear to operate primarily as redistribution mechanisms across regions rather than as instruments to offset differences in tax capacity.

title: Preventing Avoidable Medicaid and SNAP Coverage Loss: A Benefit Continuity Triage Framework

detail.title: Preventing Avoidable Medicaid and SNAP Coverage Loss: A Benefit Continuity Triage Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper does not involve human subjects research or identifiable individual-level data and therefore did not require institutional review board approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
This paper proposes a Benefit Continuity Triage framework for preventing avoidable procedural coverage loss in Medicaid and SNAP. A substantial share of disenrollment from public benefit programs occurs not because individuals become substantively ineligible, but because they fail to navigate recurring administrative requirements. Expanded work and reporting requirements under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act are likely to intensify this dynamic across Medicaid and SNAP populations.

The paper identifies a structural gap in existing benefit administration: many of the operational tools needed to prevent avoidable disenrollment already exist — including call centers, automated verification systems, digital enrollment infrastructure, community-based outreach networks, and AI-assisted navigation tools — but no coordination layer connects these systems to a common continuity-risk signal before coverage loss occurs. The proposed framework addresses this gap through four sequential components: continuous monitoring of administrative signals associated with procedural disenrollment risk, participant-level risk scoring using existing administrative data, three-tier stratification based on estimated procedural risk, and targeted intervention through existing agency infrastructure.

The framework is grounded in evidence from Medicaid unwinding and prior work requirement implementation. In Arkansas, more than 18,000 individuals lost Medicaid coverage within months of work requirement implementation, primarily for procedural rather than substantive reasons. In Georgia, active enrollment in the Pathways program remains far below the estimated eligible population, with administrative barriers identified as the primary driver of non-enrollment rather than substantive ineligibility. During Medicaid unwinding, states with stronger automated verification and ex parte renewal capacity experienced substantially lower procedural disenrollment rates than states relying more heavily on participant-facing documentation processes.

New York City — with approximately 4.5 million Medicaid enrollees, 1.5 million SNAP participants, and substantial operational infrastructure spanning DOHMH, DSS, HRA, and OHIP — is proposed as a proof-of-concept implementation site. The missing layer is not capacity. It is coordination.

The proposed approach does not require new eligibility rules, new federal authority, or large-scale technology procurement. It requires a governance decision to use existing administrative data proactively and to operationalize continuity management as a shared cross-agency responsibility.

title: Credit Supply, Firms, and Earnings Inequality
affiliations: Columbia University, University of Bonn, Bavarian State Office for Statistics (Bayerisches Landesamt für Statistik) and Government of the Federal Republic of Germany - Institute for Employment Research (IAB)

detail.title: Credit Supply, Firms, and Earnings Inequality
detail.abstract: We study the distributional consequences of monetary policy-induced credit supply in the German labor market. Firms in relationships with banks that are more exposed to the introduction of negative interest rates in 2014 experience a relative contraction in credit supply, associated with lower average wages. Within firms, initially lower-paid workers are more likely to leave employment, while initially higher-paid workers see a relative decline in wages. Between firms, wages fall by more at initially higher-paying employers. Our results suggest that credit affects the distribution of wages and employment both within and between firms.

title: Geospatial Agentic Services: A Framework for Interoperable Geospatial Intelligence in the Era of Autonomous GIS
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University, Pennsylvania State University, Pennsylvania State University, Pennsylvania State University, Emory University, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, , Government of the United States of America - US Geological Survey, Arizona State University, George Mason University - NSF Spatiotemporal Innovation Center, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and Open Geospatial Consortium

detail.title: Geospatial Agentic Services: A Framework for Interoperable Geospatial Intelligence in the Era of Autonomous GIS
detail.abstract: Autonomous GIS uses large language models as its reasoning core to automate spatial data collection, analysis, modeling, and visualization for solving spatial problems with minimal human intervention. Often implemented through autonomous geospatial agents that work independently or collaboratively, it represents a shift from GIS as a passive software environment requiring expert operation toward systems capable of task-oriented interaction, workflow generation, and increasingly autonomous spatial analysis and decision support. However, current GIS agents are often isolated and tightly coupled with specific platforms, tools, or applications, which limits their sharing, reuse, and interoperability across systems and domains. In this paper, we introduce Geospatial Agentic Services, or GAS, as a service-oriented framework for publishing, discovering, invoking, and composing GIS agents as interoperable geospatial services. GAS extends geospatial interoperability beyond access to data and predefined operations toward agentic geospatial workflows, where GIS agents function as discoverable, reusable, and collaborative service entities that encapsulate spatial knowledge and reasoning. Building on service-oriented architecture and the A2A protocol, GAS supports structured geospatial skill declarations, agentic service registry and discovery, and distributed agent orchestration. It also integrates validation, provenance, reproducibility, and governance to support transparent and trustworthy geospatial analyses. To demonstrate the framework, we prototyped a GAS platform with six GIS agents and four orchestrated workflows. By connecting traditional geospatial service architecture with emerging agentic interoperability, GAS provides a conceptual and architectural foundation for interoperable, reusable, and scalable agentic geospatial services and workflows in the era of Autonomous GIS.

title: Liquidity Trap in an International Heterogeneous Agent Framework
affiliations: Renmin University of China and Renmin University of China - School of Finance

detail.title: Liquidity Trap in an International Heterogeneous Agent Framework
detail.abstract: We provide a continuous time framework for studying liquidity trap episodes in international heterogeneous-agent incomplete-market settings. Comparing the consequences of credit tightening and demand shocks, we show that while terms of trade dynamics look qualitatively similar, the “interest rate overshooting” phenomenon identified in Guerrieri and Lorenzoni (2017) only shows up in the credit tightening case. We use our framework to illustrate both aggregate and distributional effects of the ZLB constraint, as well as the trade-offs facing capital control policy. Numerical experiments suggest that a binding ZLB constraint can have substantial implications for the design of capital control policy.

title: China, Commodities, and Chokepoints: Market Signals in an Age of Geopolitical Disruption
affiliations: Premia Research LLC

detail.title: China, Commodities, and Chokepoints: Market Signals in an Age of Geopolitical Disruption
detail.abstract: China's demand is the dominant variable in global metals pricing and a major driver of global energy prices under normal market conditions. The current moment, however, is defined by a historic supply shock: the Iran war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which the International Energy Agency has called the largest oil supply disruption in history. This brief article examines both dimensions of today's commodity landscape. It traces China's role in global price formation across crude oil, iron ore, and lithium carbonate, and then turns to the acute disruption now reshaping energy markets. The article concludes with practical guidance for institutional investors and chief investment officers on inflation-hedging, real-asset diversification, and risk monitoring in an environment of potentially multi-year energy disruption.

title: After D-day? Destruction, Catch up, and Leapfrog
affiliations: Université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne,  and Université Paris Saclay

detail.title: After D-day? Destruction, Catch up, and Leapfrog
detail.abstract: How do conflicts shape territories in the long run? To answer this question, this paper dissects population dynamics within Normandy throughout the 20th century. Despite the destruction caused by the 1944 Allied Landings, Normandy reversed the demographic decline it had experienced until 1940 — a dynamic at odds with previous literature showing a negative or neutral effect of conflicts. Using a difference-in-differences estimator, we confirm that within Normandy, combat duration dampened population growth in the short run. In the medium run, areas exposed to combat recovered and later overshot the population levels implied by their initial trend. An analysis of a comprehensive inventory of all dwelling units 25 years after WWII suggests that the post-war reconstruction effort explains this counterintuitive pattern. These results evidence the importance of reconstruction policies after conflicts. Beyond geographic fundamentals and random factors, they carve the spatial distribution of economic activities.

title: When Religion Shapes Redistribution: Islamic Economic Provisions and Income Inequality
affiliations: Pusan National University and

detail.title: When Religion Shapes Redistribution: Islamic Economic Provisions and Income Inequality
detail.abstract: This study examines how constitutionally embedded Islamic economic principles – declarations of an “Islamic Economy Provision,” “Islamic Alms/Zakat Provision,” and “Islamic Riba Provision” – aﬀect income inequality in OIC (Organisation of Islamic Cooperation) countries over the period 1980–2019. Using novel disaggregated constitutional data (Gouda, 2026) merged with World Inequality Database measures, we estimate correlated random-eﬀects panel models with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors. The results reveal heterogeneous post-2011 Arab Spring eﬀects. Broad economy declarations and Islamic alms/zakat provisions are associated with higher top-10 and top-1 income shares and compressed middle and bottom shares in Arab states, suggesting elite capture in rentier contexts. By contrast, riba prohibitions reduce Gini coeﬃcients and increase bottom-50 income shares across OIC countries. In non-Arab OIC countries, Islamic economy and alms provisions are associated with more egalitarian outcomes. The ﬁndings show that constitutional provisions operate as autonomous distributional forces, but their eﬀects are mediated by textual speciﬁcity, implementation capacity, and political context. The policy implication is that enforceable institutional mechanisms are more likely than symbolic constitutional commitments to translate Islamic egalitarian norms into redistribution.

title: Two Pathways: How Infrastructure Shapes Democratic Regime Type Through Ideology and Institutional Demand

detail.title: Two Pathways: How Infrastructure Shapes Democratic Regime Type Through Ideology and Institutional Demand

declarations.ethicsApproval: The author used publicly accessible databases and did not interview anyone.
declarations.funderStatement: The author funded the research independently.

detail.abstract: Paper P2 established that infrastructure-layer configuration is the primary cross-national predictor of democratic regime type. This paper examines how that effect operates-the causal pathways by which productive configuration shapes political institutions. Cultural materialism specifies that infrastructure exercises its effects on political structure through two analytically separable mechanisms: an ideology-mediated pathway in which infrastructure shapes emic beliefs, values, and political identities, which in turn generate institutional demand; and a direct institutional demand pathway in which infrastructure shapes the material interests, coalition structure, and selectorate geometry of political actors without passing through ideological formation first. Using a path-analytic framework applied to World Values Survey data (65 countries, N ≈ 87,000 respondents), V-Dem regime scores, and cross-national infrastructure measures, I estimate that 53 percent of infrastructure's total effect on democratic regime type operates through the ideologymediated pathway and 47 percent through direct institutional demand (Sobel z = 3.20, p = .001). These proportions are stable across alternative mediator specifications and are consistent with three independent lines of supporting evidence: the 50-year U.S. GSS partisan realignment trajectory, the Soviet natural experiment, and the phase-diagnostic analysis of the U.S. case. The finding has implications for the relative tractability of the two pathways as targets for democratic restoration: direct institutional demand responds to structural change; ideological formation responds more slowly and through different mechanisms.

title: The Board Accountability Gap in Deepfake and Synthetic Media Governance: A Proposed Interdisciplinary Governance Assessment Framework for Quantifying Board-Level Liability Across Three Synthetic Media Exposure Vectors

detail.abstract: In February 2024, the finance director of a Hong Kong multinational authorised a transfer of HK$200 million-approximately £20 million-following a video conference call with what he believed was the company's Chief Financial Officer. Every participant on that call was a deepfake. The meeting was entirely synthetic. No authentication protocol existed. No governance framework required one. The fraud succeeded because the board had never asked whether it could defend against an attack that had been technically feasible for three years. This is not an isolated failure of technology. It is a structural failure of governance-and it is being replicated, invisibly and without financial measurement, across UK organisations that deploy, commission, and receive AI-generated synthetic media without board-level frameworks capable of identifying, quantifying, or mitigating the resulting exposure. The deepfake fraud market exceeded $12.3 billion globally in 2023. Voice clone fraud is the fastest-growing fraud vector in UK financial services. The EU AI Act full compliance deadline for synthetic content obligations is August 2026. The UK AI Bill will introduce director personal liability for AI governance failures in summer 2026. UK boards are not ready. This paper introduces PADMG-the Picken AI Deepfake and Synthetic Media Governance Assessment-the first financially grounded, board-level governance framework for synthetic media risk. PADMG makes three novel contributions to the governance literature. First, it establishes the three-vector exposure framework-inbound threat, outbound liability, and thirdparty dependency-as the correct analytical architecture for board-level synthetic media governance, replacing the fragmented single-vector approaches of existing technical, legal, and communications frameworks. Second, it introduces the Deepfake Exposure Index (DEI)-the first financially quantified, board-level measure of synthetic media exposure, expressed in GBP at a stated confidence interval and directly comparable to Value at Risk in market risk governance. Third, it introduces the Synthetic Media Governance Score (SMGS)-a 0-100 board-level governance score with full regulatory interpretation at each band, providing the standardised accountability metric that regulators, insurers, and courts require but no existing framework supplies. Applied to a synthetic composite UK organisation operating across financial services and media production, PADMG identifies £324,400 in quantified governance exposure across five pillarsexposure that is entirely invisible to the board's existing governance architecture and sits in coverage gaps between cyber, fraud, and professional indemnity insurance policies. The structural forms of all PADMG models are published in full. All calibration parameters are proprietary to The Picken Governance Institute and are not disclosed.

title: When Deterrence Fails: Evidence from a Large-scale Disruption in Traffic Enforcement
affiliations: Sao Paulo School of Economics FGV EESP

detail.title: When Deterrence Fails: Evidence from a Large-scale Disruption in Traffic Enforcement
detail.abstract:
Between late 2021 and early 2024, São Paulo's automated traffic enforcement system collapsed following contract expirations and procurement failures, leaving the city without effective speed and red-light camera coverage for over two years. This paper uses this administrative disruption as a natural experiment to estimate the causal effect of suspending enforcement on road safety and to document what happens when deterrence is not reinstated even after monitoring resumes. 
     Using difference-indifferences models comparing motorcycle fatalities to those of other road users, we find that motorcyclist deaths rose by approximately 22% during the enforcement blackout and remained elevated, increasing to 30% after cameras were reactivated. This persistence reflects behavioral hysteresis: riskier riding patterns formed under low enforcement did not reverse when monitoring returned. Over a 49-month window, we estimate approximately 300 excess motorcycle fatalities attributable to the disruption. Our cost-benefit calculation shows that the social cost of these deaths, totaling approximately R$ 370 million, exceeds the public expenditure savings from reduced camera coverage by approximately 40%. 
      Triple-difference analysis, applied to citation data, reveals that the behavioral shift is concentrated in bus lane encroachment and red-light running-rather than speeding, consistent with deliberate risk-taking rather than incidental exposure. The spatial analysis further shows that fatality increases are concentrated in peripheral districts with higher socioeconomic vulnerability and lower baseline enforcement coverage, underscoring the distributional consequences of enforcement failure. 
     These findings have direct implications for urban road safety governance. First, the continuity of enforcement is an investment in public health: the proper maintenance of mechanisms creates credibility, and the costs of interruption far outweigh the apparent government operational savings. Second, deterrence is not fully reversible: reinstating enforcement contracts restores citations but not compliance. The new behavioral equilibrium does not dissolve when monitoring resumes. And lastly, the drop in enforcement has a greater impact on the most vulnerable segments of the population, motorcycle users, and those most concentrated in the city's peripheries. The evidence points to the need to treat automated enforcement contracts as critical public infrastructure, subject to continuity requirements analogous to those governing essential services.

title: The End of History, Revisited: A Compound Civilizational Stress Event, the AI Governance Window, and the 10% Path

detail.title: The End of History, Revisited: A Compound Civilizational Stress Event, the AI Governance Window, and the 10% Path

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no financial conflicts of interest. Research was conducted independently through UX Minds, LLC.
declarations.funderStatement: Unfunded independent research.

detail.abstract:
This essay constitutes a multi-framework civilizational analysis of Francis Fukuyama's End of History thesis, interrogating whether liberal democracy's theoretical endpoint has proven achievable, or whether humanity has reached, and is retreating from, the maximum complexity of political organization its cognitive and institutional architecture can sustain.

Drawing on eight converging theoretical frameworks: Fukuyama, Huntington, Polanyi, Gramsci, Schumpeter, Arendt, Wallerstein, and Habermas, with Varoufakis's techno-feudalism supplying the structural economic diagnosis, the analysis argues the current moment is best understood as a compound civilizational stress event: multiple historical forces arriving simultaneously, without institutional capacity sufficient to manage any one of them.

The essay develops four probability-ranked trajectories and works backward from the conditions democratic renewal requires, identifying three tiers of defensive action. The AI governance layer receives extended treatment as the most consequential long-term variable, distinguishing the current mechanism through three structural properties: optimization without intent, personalization at scale with feedback closure, and a speed-deliberation asymmetry no longer compensable by democratic effort. A governance window of approximately 3–7 years is identified before the binding-framework opportunity closes.

title: The Effects of Recent Federal Immigration Enforcement on Private Sector Employment in California and Washington, D.C
affiliations: , University of California at Merced and University of California at Merced

detail.title: The Effects of Recent Federal Immigration Enforcement on Private Sector Employment in California and Washington, D.C
detail.abstract: The UC Merced Community and Labor Center analyzed Current Population Survey data for the periods before and following escalations in federal immigration enforcement actions in California and Washington, D.C. The Center examined changes in the number of workers in California and the rest of the US, for the weeks of May 11, June 8, July 6, and August 10, 2025, and found that the greatest decrease in persons reporting private sector work coincided with peak escalations in federal immigration enforcement. In Washington, D.C., persons reporting private sector work decreased by 3.3% in August, similar to California's decrease of 3.1% from May to June 2025. Findings indicate the effect of escalated immigration enforcement actions on work is comparable with the Great Recession and the COVID-19 pandemic. Ongoing escalated immigration enforcement actions suggest the need for policy interventions to mitigate negative economic consequences.

title: Fish Farming, Nutrition and Food security in Manipur: Production Gaps and Farm-level Economics
affiliations: College Of Agriculture, Indira Gandhi Krishi Vishwavidyalaya, Dept of Agricultural Economics, CAU, Imphal and Indira Gandhi krishi Vishwavidyalaya, Raipur

detail.title: Fish Farming, Nutrition and Food security in Manipur: Production Gaps and Farm-level Economics
detail.abstract: Background: Fisheries were recognized as a key nutrition-sensitive food system contributing to food security, dietary protein intake, and rural livelihood resilience, particularly in regions with high dependence on fish as a primary animal-source food. In Manipur, fish played a central role in dietary nutrition, making its production and accessibility critical for nutrition security. Aims: The study aimed to examine fisheries development in Manipur by linking inland fish production patterns and resource availability with farm-level economic performance to understand its implications for food and nutrition security. Study design: The study adopted a mixed-method approach combining secondary data analysis with primary farm-level survey data. Place and Duration of Study: The study was conducted in Manipur, India, focusing on Bishnupur and Imphal West districts, which are major fish-producing areas of the state. The study period covered 2022-23. Methodology: Secondary data were used to assess inland water resource availability, fish production trends, and demand-supply gaps in fish as a key source of dietary animal protein. Primary data were collected from 96 fish farmers using a structured interview schedule to examine input use, cost structure, production practices, and income generation. Standard cost concepts (Cost A₁, Cost B, and Cost C) were applied to estimate cost of cultivation. Farm-level economic indicators such as gross income, net income, and benefitcost ratio were computed to evaluate profitability and its implications for nutrition-sensitive food production systems. Results: The study found that Manipur possessed 56,461.05 hectares of inland water resources, of which only 39% was utilized for fish culture, indicating substantial underutilization of nutrition-relevant production resources. This resulted in a fish production deficit of 19,480 tonnes relative to estimated demand, highlighting a structural gap in dietary protein availability. Fish production was concentrated in valley districts, particularly Bishnupur and Imphal West, reflecting regional disparities in access to nutrition-supporting food systems. Farm-level analysis showed that the total cost of fish production was ₹105,483.60 per hectare, while gross and net returns were ₹198,592.80 and ₹93,109.20 per hectare, respectively. The benefit-cost ratio of 1.88 indicated strong economic viability of fish farming as a nutrition-supporting livelihood activity. Polyculture systems contributed significantly to both income generation and dietary protein supply. Conclusion: The study concluded that although fish farming was economically viable and contributed to nutrition-sensitive food supply, underutilization of resources and spatial disparities limited its full contribution to food and nutrition security. Expanding aquaculture through improved resource utilization and balanced regional development could enhance availability of affordable animal protein, strengthen rural livelihoods, and improve nutrition security in Manipur.

title: Impairments of Investment Securities by Nonfinancial Firms
affiliations: University of Connecticut - Department of Accounting, City University of New York (CUNY) - Stan Ross Department of Accountancy and University of Connecticut - Department of Accounting

detail.title: Impairments of Investment Securities by Nonfinancial Firms
detail.abstract: We study other-than-temporary impairments (OTTI) of investment securities in nonfinancial firms. Although these firms hold debt and equity securities, accounting rules and related academic research focus predominantly on financial institutions. We document the frequency and nature of OTTI among S&P 1,500 nonfinancial firms during 2000—2013. Exploring the recognition drivers in the relevant rules, we find that, consistent with the objective of regulation in effect during the period, the propensity to report OTTI is associated with variables capturing the likelihood of having impaired investments and the intent and ability to hold these investments to recovery. We find no evidence of opportunistic reporting. We also document an association between OTTI and earnings announcement returns, suggesting investors found the recognition of OTTI informative. Finally, we provide preliminary evidence that nonfinancial firms may have restructured their investment holdings in response to the promulgation of ASU 2016-01 and ASU 2016-13, which modified the accounting for investment securities for all public US firms. Our findings contribute to the policy-relevant discussion of the costs and benefits associated with industry-agnostic versus sector-specific standards.

title: Physics-aware feature engineering improves spatial transferability of satellite estuarine salinity models: a Mekong Delta evaluation
affiliations: Vietnam National University - Ho Chi Minh City (VNU-HCM) - University of Science, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Vietnam National University - Ho Chi Minh City (VNU-HCM) - University of Science

detail.title: Physics-aware feature engineering improves spatial transferability of satellite estuarine salinity models: a Mekong Delta evaluation
detail.abstract: Estuarine surface salinity controls freshwater availability, but dissolved salt is non-optically active and cannot be directly observed by satellites. Satellite models rely on indirect proxies (e.g., colored dissolved organic matter, suspended sediment, roughness), whose covariance with salinity varies across flow regimes. Most models report high accuracy under weakly structured validation, which leaks spatial structure and fails to test generalization to unmonitored stations. We tested whether physics-aware predictors improve spatial transferability of Random Forest salinity models across 21 Mekong Delta stations during the 2016–2023 dry seasons. The workflow combines discharge, tidal statistics, and discharge-position interaction terms with Harmonized Landsat–Sentinel-2 and Sentinel-1 predictors, using a square-root target transform to reduce freshwater smoothing. Spectral-only models performed weakly under strict leave-one-station-out (LOSO) validation (R^2 = 0.26, RMSE = 5.33 PSU). Adding forcing and interaction terms raised LOSO skill to R^2 = 0.60 (RMSE = 3.93 PSU), leave-one-year-out R^2 = 0.67, and forward temporal R^2 = 0.78. Boundary regularization using hydrodynamic pseudo-observations improved freshwater predictions without inflating validation metrics. SHAP attribution confirmed that discharge-position interactions are the dominant predictors, behaving consistently with estuarine salt-wedge dynamics. Freshwater and saline-regime errors are reported separately because global RMSE can hide upstream overprediction. The resulting maps accurately represent dry-season, station-supported lower-estuary reaches within the river-only domain.

title: HeteroPlace: Resource-Aware Placement for Heterogeneous FPGAs with Reinforcement Learning
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Hubei University of Technology, Central China Normal University, Hubei University of Technology, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: HeteroPlace: Resource-Aware Placement for Heterogeneous FPGAs with Reinforcement Learning
detail.abstract: Modern FPGAs contain highly heterogeneous resources, such as CLBs, RAMs, and DSPs, whose non-uniform spatial distributions pose significant challenges for efficient placement. Although electrostatics-based frameworks such as ePlace and DREAMPlace have achieved strong results in ASIC placement, directly applying them to FPGAs is difficult because FPGA placement must satisfy resource compatibility and architectural site constraints. To address these challenges, this paper presents HeteroPlace, a unified FPGA placement framework designed to handle heterogeneous resource distributions across different FPGA architectures and benchmark designs. HeteroPlace introduces resource-aware density maps for different resource types, enabling the global placer to guide instances toward compatible resource regions and away from incompatible regions during optimization. In addition, HeteroPlace employs a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agent to dynamically adjust the density weight. This adaptive control mechanism replaces fixed or manually tuned density weight and improves robustness across designs with different scales, netlist structures, and resource distributions. Experimental results on industrial heterogeneous FPGA benchmarks show that HeteroPlace consistently reduces legalized HPWL compared with several state-of-the-art methods and achieves competitive or better results than an industrial QP-based placer.

title: Bayesian Updating with Multivariate Machine Learning-based Prior and Spatial Geostatistics-based Likelihood for Posterior Predictions of Unconventional Reservoir Performance
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin, University of Texas at Austin, University of Texas at Austin, affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Texas at Austin

detail.title: Bayesian Updating with Multivariate Machine Learning-based Prior and Spatial Geostatistics-based Likelihood for Posterior Predictions of Unconventional Reservoir Performance
detail.abstract: Accurate forecasting of hydrocarbon production in unconventional reservoirs requires integrating spatial heterogeneity with well-scale geological and engineering data. Traditional machine learning regression approaches often neglect spatial context, including spatial continuity, spatial trends and data locations, resulting in potential overestimation of uncertainty. To address this limitation, we introduce a Bayesian updating workflow with a multivariate machine learning model as a prior model and a spatial geostatistical model of well production as a likelihood model. The workflow is applied after normal score transformation of all features in Gaussian space to provide complete local uncertainty models from geostatistical kriging estimates and variances and to facilitate the use of closed-form analytical Bayesian updating. Our proposed workflow is demonstrated with 9 geological and 6 completion secondary features to forecast cumulative one-year oil production as the primary feature for an unconventional reservoir. A multivariate machine learning-based prior model is first calculated using local ridge regression with hyperparameter tuning to relate the secondary features to production. The likelihood model is calculated by ordinary kriging based on an additive deterministic trend and residual estimation. Bayesian updating with K-fold cross-validation is then applied to tune the workflow, demonstrating a reduction of the high uncertainty of the prior model, yielding a posterior distribution that is both more accurate and precise than the machine learning or geostatistical distributions on their own.

title: Information Frictions, Data Factor Agglomeration, and Cross-Regional Corporate Investment
affiliations: Jiangxi University of Finance and Economics, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Jiangxi University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Information Frictions, Data Factor Agglomeration, and Cross-Regional Corporate Investment
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether data factor agglomeration promotes cross-regional corporate investment by reducing information frictions. Using a firm–destination–year panel of Chinese listed firms from 2010 to 2022, we exploit regional variation generated by the rollout of National Big Data Comprehensive Pilot Zones to identify the effect of data factor agglomeration on cross-regional corporate investment. The results show that data factor agglomeration significantly increases firms' investment in non-local destinations, suggesting that data-related institutions can facilitate spatial capital mobility. Mechanism analyses suggest that the effect operates through lower financing constraints, higher operating efficiency, and a more competitive market environment. The effect is stronger for non-state-owned firms, smaller-scale investments, and firms with higher digital dependence. These findings highlight the role of data-related institutional reforms in reducing spatial information frictions and shaping the geography of corporate investment.

title: Artificial intelligence and supply chain concentration: Evidence from focal firms in China
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU), affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Artificial intelligence and supply chain concentration: Evidence from focal firms in China

keywords: Supply chain concentration；Dynamic capabilities；Supply chain concentration

detail.abstract: While artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into business operations, its ripple effects across inter-firm production networks remain underexplored. Integrating the theories of dynamic capabilities and production networks, this study investigates how AI adoption by focal firms reshapes their network structures, specifically focusing on its impact on supply chain concentration. Analyzing panel data from A-share listed companies in China from 2010 to 2023, our evidence suggests that AI adoption significantly reduces supply chain concentration, facilitating partner diversification. Mechanistically, this reduction is achieved by lowering operational costs and improving operational efficiency, which empowers firms to expand their partner networks. The results also show an asymmetric distribution, with the de-concentration effect being more pronounced in SOEs and non-high-tech firms; for non-SOEs, only upstream reductions and increases in downstream concentration for high-tech firms. These findings offer new insights into AI-driven strategic positioning and offer theoretical and managerial implications for supply chain resilience.

title: Does Measurement Bias Explain Sex Differences in Self-Reported Empathy?
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Rethink Priorities, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Independent Researcher, , University of Tokyo and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Does Measurement Bias Explain Sex Differences in Self-Reported Empathy?
detail.abstract: Self-reports of trait empathic concern suggest that females are more empathic than males, whereas state empathy reports show smaller, inconsistent sex differences. Researchers have interpreted this pattern as evidence that sex differences in trait empathy reflect biases elicited by personality questionnaires but not real-time reports of emotional experience. However, trait and state measures assess empathy at different levels of aggregation, and the hypothesis that trait measures are more biased than state measures has never been tested. We conducted measurement invariance analyses across eleven studies (N = 6,832). Non-invariance effects on observed sex differences were small, although trait measures failed invariance tests more often than state measures. Meta-analytic latent estimates indicated that females reported greater state and trait empathy than males.

title: Beyond Factory Walls: Women’s Employment Opportunity, Inter-industry Spillovers and Gender Gap in Manufacturing Employment
affiliations: University of Dhaka

detail.title: Beyond Factory Walls: Women’s Employment Opportunity, Inter-industry Spillovers and Gender Gap in Manufacturing Employment
detail.abstract: The gender employment gap in the manufacturing sector, mainly due to lower female participation, is a key obstacle to economic growth in low- and lower-middle-income countries. This paper examines whether job opportunities for women in a particular industry can narrow the gender employment gap in that industry as well as in other manufacturing industries. I measure female employment opportunities in terms of people’s geographic proximity to an export-oriented, female-intensive manufacturing industry. I compare manufacturing employment across individuals by gender and spatial proximity and find that the gender gap in manufacturing employment decreases as individuals live near the factories in that industry. Analysis of within- and across-industry effects suggests that spatial exposure to the export factories significantly reduces the gender employment gap not only in the said export industry but also in other female-intensive non-export manufacturing industries. These results support the notion that women’s employment opportunities can help increase manufacturing employment, which can contribute to economic growth by narrowing the associated gender employment gap.

title: Towards a Safety Copilot: Predicting and Interpreting Risky Non-Motorist Behaviors with a Fine-Tuned Large Language Model
affiliations: Tongji University, Lund University, University of Massachusetts Lowell, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Tongji University, Tongji University and Tongji University

detail.title: Towards a Safety Copilot: Predicting and Interpreting Risky Non-Motorist Behaviors with a Fine-Tuned Large Language Model
detail.abstract: Non‐motorist fatalities represent a substantial and growing share of U.S. traffic deaths. These incidents are driven by complex, context-dependent risky behaviors such as failure to yield, improper crossings, and inattentiveness. Predicting these behaviors and their collision outcomes remains a critical challenge for advanced driver-assistance and traffic safety systems. This study introduces a copilot safety framework that reframes accident prediction as a text-reasoning task, leveraging a fine-tuned large language model (LLM) to jointly predict risky non-motorist behavior, vehicle–non-motorist collision angle, and number of fatalities from structured accident narratives. We fine-tune Llama 3.1 8B with Low-Rank Adaptation on 69,719 fatal accident records from the Fatality Analysis Reporting System (2015–2023), converting each incident into a natural-language prompt that includes several categories of context: general accident information, non‐motorist demographics, environmental conditions, weather, traffic maneuvers, road surface information, and vehicle details. On a held-out test set, the fine-tuned LLM achieves the highest predictive performance among all models across all three tasks, but absolute performance is low for the challenging 10‐class non‐motorist behavior task. For collision angle, the LLM attains high accuracy but a much lower macro F1 due to severe class imbalance, while for single vs. multiple fatality classification, it achieves near‐perfect scores. Shapley value analysis reveals that the LLM’s feature attributions agree in sign with a logistic regression benchmark in approximately 70% of feature–class pairs overall; however, when restricting to statistically significant logit coefficients, 18 direct sign conflicts emerge, concentrated in complex accident types (e.g., side impacts, improper turns) and low‐prevalence classes. A prototype deployment integrating a vision-language model (VLM) with the LLM copilot demonstrates the feasibility of extracting real-world scenario descriptors from pre-accident video and generating interpretable, feature‐attributed predictions. The findings highlight that while fine‐tuned LLMs can outperform traditional methods on several accident prediction tasks, they still struggle with highly imbalanced, linguistically subtle behaviors, and their post‐hoc explanations may hallucinate directionally incorrect effects for safety‐critical features. Improving data quality, class balance, and explanation faithfulness remains essential before such models can inform driver warnings or engineering countermeasures.

title: (De-)Radicalizing the Radical Right with Slanted News on Immigration
affiliations: University of Vienna and University of Vienna

detail.title: (De-)Radicalizing the Radical Right with Slanted News on Immigration
detail.abstract: Radical Right (RR) political parties have become increasingly radicalized on immigration across many developed countries. We study whether exposure to slanted (i.e., one-sided) news shifts policy views of RR voters on immigration in Austria. In an online experiment, participants received slanted news about the effects of immigration on the welfare state. We find that anti-immigration news further radicalizes RR voters by reinforcing extreme policy views, while slanted pro-immigration news has no de-radicalizing effect. Surprisingly, balanced news — presenting both sides — reduces radicalization. We show that balanced news coverage increases trust, thereby increasing RR voters’ receptiveness to opposing viewpoints.

title: Divided We Act: The Role of Social Sanctions in a Polarized World
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania, Stanford University,  and University of Nottingham

detail.title: Divided We Act: The Role of Social Sanctions in a Polarized World
detail.abstract: Social sanctions sustain social order by reinforcing widely accepted principles. Political polarization may weaken this mechanism by fragmenting these principles, yet causal effects are hard to identify: observational data cannot separate the effect of polarized preferences from exposure to polarization. We model theoretically and test experimentally the effectiveness of social sanctions in a representative U.S. sample (N = 2,400) that exogenously varies environmental polarization. Participants allocate money between politically opposed recipients privately and publicly, and public allocations can be punished by partisan Observers drawn from distributions varying in their degree of polarization. With greater polarization, public allocations become less equitable because participants (correctly) expect punishment even when acting fairly. This shows that polarization causally undermines the disciplining role of social sanctions.

title: Gender Representation and Collective Decision-Making in Expert Committees
affiliations: Monash University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Gender Representation and Collective Decision-Making in Expert Committees
detail.abstract: This paper studies how gender representation affects collective decision-making in expert committees. I exploit quasi-random assignment of judges to panels in the Greek Supreme Court using newly digitized data on 3,700 criminal appeals. I find that panels with more female judges are more likely to reject appeals and less likely to delegate cases. Effects are nonlinear and emerge primarily once at least three of five judges are female; below this level, representation has no detectable effect. The mechanism appears to operate at the panel rather than the individual level — panels with a higher share of female judges take significantly longer to decide, especially in complex cases and in familiar panel compositions, consistent with more thorough deliberation rather than coordination costs. These findings suggest that diversity policies targeting modest increases in female representation will have limited impact unless they shift the deliberative composition of the group itself.

title: Immigration Enforcement Visibility and Consumer Spending
affiliations: , City University New York (CUNY), Queens College and

detail.title: Immigration Enforcement Visibility and Consumer Spending
detail.abstract: We exploit the sharp escalation in community-based ICE enforcement following the January 2025 inauguration to estimate the causal effect of immigration enforcement on consumer spending. Using Synthetic Difference-in-Differences with cross-state variation in surge intensity as the identifying variation, we find that states experiencing the largest enforcement surges saw aggregate card spending decline by 1.7 percentage points relative to their SDiD counterfactual, an effect robust to covariate adjustment, alternative shock windows, and pre-tariff truncation. Null estimates for non-in-person spending rule out a broad regional demand shock, while null estimates for jail-based arrests (enforcement invisible to surrounding communities) isolate enforcement visibility as the operative mechanism. Sector-level estimates reveal two empirically distinct channels: in states with Democratic governors, aggregate spending fell by −4.1 pp (p < 0.01), driven by large declines in Accommodation and Food Services (−2.3 pp) and Arts, Entertainment, and Recreation (−7.3 pp), consistent with behavioral withdrawal from public commercial life in jurisdictions where community enforcement was most visible. In Trump-voting states, Home Improvement Centers and Transportation and Warehousing spending fell by −3.8 pp (p < 0.1) and −3.0 pp (p < 0.01) respectively, consistent with labor supply disruption among undocumented workers in construction and logistics. Our results indicate that the economic costs of enforcement extend well beyond the directly targeted population and depend critically on whether enforcement is visible to the surrounding community — not merely on its scale.

title: Indirect Estimators of Intergenerational Mobility
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: Indirect Estimators of Intergenerational Mobility
detail.abstract: This chapter reviews indirect estimators of intergenerational mobility, focusing on approaches that infer parent–child or other family associations when direct income data are incomplete or unavailable. We synthesize methods based on instrumental variables, imputation using observable characteristics such as education and occupation, surname-based estimators, and multigenerational linkages. To unify these approaches, we introduce a stylized framework in which socioeconomic status is transmitted through multiple pathways with heterogeneous persistence rates. Within this framework, both direct and indirect estimators can be interpreted as weighted averages of these underlying transmission channels. A central insight is that the choice of instrument or imputation strategy determines these weights, leading different methods to capture distinct aspects of the transmission process. We highlight implications for interpretation, showing that indirect estimators need not recover conventional parent–child correlations but can instead provide complementary evidence on long-run persistence and the mechanisms underlying persistent inequalities.

title: Charging the Transition: Directed Technical Change with Enabling Technologies
affiliations: and NHH Norwegian School of Economics - Department of Business and Management Science

detail.title: Charging the Transition: Directed Technical Change with Enabling Technologies
detail.abstract: We study how complementarity reshapes innovation incentives and the effectiveness of policies aimed at directing technological transitions. By incorporating energy storage into a macro-climate model, we show that when this enabling technology lags behind renewables, advances in renewable technology can paradoxically reduce incentives for clean innovation. We analytically characterize this novel indirect path dependency effect, which provides a new explanation for the post-2010 collapse in renewable patenting. Calibrated to the U.S. economy, we find that omitting storage overestimates climate policy effectiveness, optimal policy should prioritize storage over renewables, and halving the storage productivity gap increases annual welfare by 1%.

title: The ifo Business Climate Index for Germany: A Vintage Dataset
affiliations: Ifo Institute and Ifo Institute

detail.title: The ifo Business Climate Index for Germany: A Vintage Dataset
detail.abstract: The ifo Business Climate Index for Germany is one of the most widely used leading indicators for the German economy. This paper introduces a new vintage dataset that contains all originally published time series of the ifo Business Climate Index and its components since January 2004. The dataset covers eight sectors - including the aggregate indicators for Overall Economy and Industry and Trade as well as six sectoral indicators - each with three time series for business climate, current business situation, and business expectations. It documents the historical evolution of the index across publication vintages and captures revisions arising from seasonal adjustment and from methodological changes, such as the transition to the X-13ARIMA-SEATS seasonal adjustment method in 2015 and the inclusion of the service sector in 2018. A revision analysis covering the period from April 2018 onward shows that first-release values are highly reliable: mean revisions are close to zero across all series, and the directional signal of the month-on-month change is confirmed by subsequent vintages in more than nine out of ten months for the headline indicator. The dataset is publicly available at https://www.ifo.de/ifo-zeitreihen and enables a wide range of further research, including real-time forecasting exercises, turning-point analyses, and studies of financial market reactions to initial data releases.
